title: Understanding Depression and Depressive Disorders — References and source notes
text: The text is independently drafted as general public mental health education informed by these sources. This is not an official adaptation or endorsement by WHO, NIMH, or NICE. Review source permissions before republishing excerpts or translated materials.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Understanding psychological trauma
text: A potentially traumatic event is an experience involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, sexual violence, or another event perceived as profoundly threatening. Events may be sudden, repeated, witnessed, or encountered in a work setting. Examples include serious road accidents, violent attacks, conflict, disasters, severe medical emergencies and some experiences of abuse. Whether an event is traumatic for a particular person depends on the circumstances and its effects; no one should have to prove that an event was “bad enough” to deserve support. Psychological trauma describes the emotional and psychological effects that may follow overwhelming or threatening experiences. A person may feel frightened, shaken, numb, angry, ashamed or disconnected. The body’s alarm system can remain highly sensitive even after the immediate danger ends. These responses are not signs of weakness or moral failure. Some people find that reactions settle with time and support; others experience longer-lasting difficulties. [1, 2]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Why people respond differently
text: Two people can live through the same event and have different reactions. Responses are shaped by prior experiences, immediate safety, severity and duration of exposure, injuries, available support, health, age, and whether ongoing threats remain. A supportive environment can help recovery, while continuing danger and social isolation can make recovery harder.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Why people respond differently
text: The majority of people who experience potentially traumatic events do not develop PTSD. WHO estimates that approximately 5.6% of people exposed to a potentially traumatic event develop PTSD, although risk differs substantially by type of exposure. This is population information, not a way to predict any individual’s outcome. [1]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Common reactions in the first days and weeks
text: Reactions are not identical for everyone. Some people feel very little at first and notice distress later. Others recover without specialist treatment. Persistent, severe, or worsening symptoms deserve assessment, even if the person appears functional at work or at home. [1, 2]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Stress responses versus a diagnosis
text: A reaction after a frightening event is not automatically a mental health disorder. In the early period, it is often most helpful to focus on practical safety, access to essential needs, supportive contact, sleep where possible, and monitoring whether distress improves. A person can seek help at any time; they do not have to wait for a diagnosis.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Stress responses versus a diagnosis
text: In clinical systems, acute stress disorder is a defined condition emerging in the first month after a qualifying event, with a particular pattern of symptoms and functional impact. PTSD involves a different set of diagnostic criteria. A clinician considers symptom timing, event history, distress, functional impairment, alternative explanations and co-occurring conditions. Self-diagnosis from a checklist is unreliable. [2, 3]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — What is PTSD?
text: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a mental health condition that can develop following exposure to one or more traumatic events. Core features include involuntary re-experiencing of the event, avoidance of reminders, and an ongoing sense of threat or heightened arousal. Symptoms must also cause significant distress or interference with ordinary activities. Additional changes in mood, thinking, memory, and relationships may occur. [1, 2]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — What is PTSD?
text: PTSD can begin soon after an event or become noticeable later. Not everyone with intrusive memories or nightmares has PTSD. Professional assessment matters because symptoms may overlap with depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, brain injury, substance-related problems or physical illness.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Re-experiencing symptoms
text: Re-experiencing means the event returns to awareness in unwanted, distressing ways. This can include intrusive memories, upsetting dreams, or flashbacks. During a flashback a person may briefly feel as though the event is happening again, rather than simply remembering it. Sounds, smells, dates or situations can sometimes act as reminders.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Re-experiencing symptoms
text: The experience can feel frightening and confusing. Trying to forcefully stop every unwanted memory may not work. When a person feels overwhelmed, gentle orientation to the current environment and professional support can be more useful than repeatedly rehearsing the traumatic event alone.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Avoidance and withdrawal
text: People may avoid places, people, conversations, feelings or activities that remind them of what happened. Avoidance can offer short-term relief, especially when the reminder is intense. However, broad avoidance of safe daily situations may gradually restrict work, travel, relationships and ordinary routines. [1, 2]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Avoidance and withdrawal
text: Avoidance must not be confused with choosing to stay away from actual danger. It is appropriate to avoid genuinely unsafe people and places. Trauma treatment can help distinguish current threats from reminders of past threats, and can address unhelpful avoidance through a carefully planned process.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Hyperarousal and feeling constantly unsafe
text: Hyperarousal describes a heightened state of alertness. A person may scan surroundings, feel “on edge,” startle at ordinary sounds, struggle to sleep, or become irritable. Concentration can be difficult when the nervous system repeatedly signals danger.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Hyperarousal and feeling constantly unsafe
text: The goal of supportive care is not to tell someone that their fear is irrational. Instead, acknowledge the experience, check present safety, and collaborate on appropriate steps. Physical complaints should be medically assessed when they are severe, unusual or unexplained.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Changes in mood, beliefs and connection
text: Trauma can affect a person’s view of themselves, other people and the world. Some people blame themselves for what happened, feel guilt or shame, lose interest in activities, or struggle to trust others. These beliefs may be shaped by danger, threats or harmful messages received during the event. None of these feelings establishes personal responsibility for an assault or other harm.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Changes in mood, beliefs and connection
text: Emotional numbness may make affection, enjoyment or connection harder. Supportive relationships and appropriate treatment can help, but a person should not be pressured to become sociable or disclose private details before they are ready.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Dissociation and feeling disconnected
text: Some people experience dissociation: feeling detached from themselves, their emotions or surroundings, or finding parts of an experience difficult to recall. A person may describe feeling unreal, emotionally absent or as if they are watching events from outside themselves. Similar experiences can also have other causes.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Dissociation and feeling disconnected
text: If someone becomes disoriented, avoid startling or touching them without permission. Speak calmly, identify yourself, offer simple present-focused choices, and seek clinical help when episodes are persistent, severe or impair functioning. Strong inward-focus or visualization activities may worsen discomfort for some people; a person should be free to stop them.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Trauma, sleep and daily functioning
text: Sleep difficulties can follow trauma, including trouble falling asleep, waking frequently, nightmares, and fatigue. Poor sleep may contribute to concentration problems, irritability and low mood. Gentle routines, an adequately safe sleeping environment, and reducing alcohol can support rest, but recurring nightmares or substantial impairment warrant assessment.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Trauma, sleep and daily functioning
text: Trauma can also affect study, work, caregiving, physical health and relationships. People may experience a mixture of distress and moments of ordinary functioning. Neither visible productivity nor the absence of tears tells us whether someone needs support.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Acute stress and early support after an event
text: In the hours or days following trauma, a supportive response begins with checking immediate safety, urgent medical needs, shelter, food, access to trusted people, and clear practical information. Offer choices and listen if the person wants to speak. Do not insist on a detailed retelling or suggest that everyone must express their emotions in a particular way.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Acute stress and early support after an event
text: A single compulsory emotional debriefing session intended to prevent PTSD is not recommended. For people who have clinically important symptoms or acute stress disorder, evidence-based trauma-focused care may be appropriate even within the first month, assessed and delivered by qualified professionals. [2, 4]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — PTSD, complex PTSD and repeated trauma
text: Some people experience repeated or prolonged traumatic events and may develop broader difficulties involving emotional regulation, sense of self and relationships, alongside the core PTSD symptoms. ICD-11 describes complex PTSD as a distinct diagnosis. This is not the same as saying that every person who experienced repeated trauma has complex PTSD.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — PTSD, complex PTSD and repeated trauma
text: Complex presentations may require flexible, coordinated care that considers current safety, housing, family responsibilities and other mental health needs. Assessment should be individualized, culturally sensitive and never based on an online label alone. [2]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Trauma across ages and contexts
text: Children may express distress through changes in behavior, sleep, separation fears, or repetitive play. Adolescents may show withdrawal, irritability, reduced school participation or risky coping behaviors. Older adults may experience trauma symptoms alongside physical illness or bereavement. These signs can have multiple explanations and should not be interpreted without context.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Trauma across ages and contexts
text: Readers supporting a child should use age-appropriate care, respect safeguarding duties and seek qualified assistance when distress persists. This adult-oriented chapter is not a trauma-treatment manual for children. [1, 2]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Practical coping: orienting to the present
text: Optional exercise - “Here and now”: (1) Look around and identify two neutral objects; (2) if comfortable, feel the chair or floor supporting you; (3) say silently, “I am noticing where I am now”; (4) choose a small action, such as drinking water or moving to a quieter place. Keep your eyes open if preferred. Stop if this increases distress or disconnection.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Practical coping: orienting to the present
text: Present-focused orientation can help some people manage temporary overwhelm. It is not an exposure therapy and does not remove the need for medical or psychological care. Not every grounding method suits every person, especially those experiencing dissociation or ongoing danger.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Practical coping: steady daily anchors
text: After trauma, large goals can feel unmanageable. A small daily anchor may include one regular meal, a short walk if safe, a predictable wake time, or checking in with a trusted person. Choose activities that are accessible and realistic, not a rigid schedule that creates more pressure.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Practical coping: steady daily anchors
text: Examples: A person recovering from a frightening road incident may begin with a quiet morning routine and help arranging transport. Someone experiencing nightmares may create a simple sleep routine and discuss persistent symptoms with a clinician. Neither person needs to “push through” overwhelming exposure on their own.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Practical coping: a supportive contact plan
text: Think of one or two people who listen respectfully and will not pressure you to disclose. Consider what kind of support you would welcome: a practical errand, accompaniment to a health visit, company, or a simple message. A trusted person is someone you choose, not necessarily a relative or authority figure.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Practical coping: a supportive contact plan
text: If privacy or personal safety is uncertain, avoid storing sensitive details where someone else can access them. Sharing a trauma history is optional for the activities in this chapter. An emergency situation calls for immediate assistance rather than a routine contact plan.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Evidence-based psychological treatment
text: There are effective treatments for PTSD. Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapies help people process trauma-related memories and beliefs, reduce disabling avoidance, and rebuild daily functioning. Examples include cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy for PTSD, prolonged exposure and narrative exposure therapy. These structured treatments are provided by trained practitioners, with monitoring and an agreed plan. [1, 2]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Evidence-based psychological treatment
text: Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) is another evidence-based option for some people with PTSD. It is a structured clinical therapy, not simply moving the eyes while recalling distressing experiences. Suitability, timing and choice of treatment depend on age, circumstances, clinical needs, preferences and available expertise. [1, 2]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Medicines and other supports
text: A qualified prescriber may recommend medication for some adults with PTSD after discussing benefits, risks, preferences and coexisting conditions. Guidelines differ by population and treatment context; medication is not a universal first-line solution. NICE advises against medicines, including benzodiazepines, for preventing PTSD after trauma. For children, treatment recommendations differ and require specialist assessment. [2]

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Medicines and other supports
text: Care can also address depression, anxiety, sleep problems, substance use difficulties, physical injuries or ongoing safety concerns. Improving living conditions and access to supportive relationships may be important alongside psychological treatment.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — When to seek professional help
text: Seek an assessment if symptoms persist, worsen, disrupt work or school, affect relationships, lead to frequent nightmares or flashbacks, or make ordinary activities very difficult. Earlier help is appropriate if symptoms are severe, even within the first month after the event. Trauma-related symptoms are treatable; someone does not need to wait until they can no longer cope.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — When to seek professional help
text: A healthcare worker can ask about symptoms without demanding a graphic recounting in an initial conversation. Assessment may include sleep, mood, functioning, personal safety, medical conditions and substance use. People can ask about confidentiality, available treatment options, costs and referral pathways.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Immediate safety and urgent warning signs
text: Urgent assistance: If a person is at immediate risk of suicide or serious self-harm, has life-threatening injuries, is in immediate danger, or is severely confused or unable to stay safe, seek emergency medical or protection assistance now. Use verified local emergency services or the nearest emergency department. This handbook does not supply unverified Rwanda hotline numbers.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Immediate safety and urgent warning signs
text: If it is safe, stay with someone at imminent risk until appropriate help arrives, and remove immediate hazards only when this can be done without placing anyone in danger. Do not promise secrecy about imminent life-threatening risk. When a person is experiencing ongoing violence or coercion, discuss safety privately with qualified support personnel; avoid actions that could expose them to further harm.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Supporting someone who has experienced trauma
text: Start by listening without judgment. Say that they can share as much or as little as they wish. Ask what would help right now and respect their decisions wherever safely possible. Offer concrete support: accompaniment to a clinic, childcare, transport, or assistance finding information. Follow through on commitments.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Supporting someone who has experienced trauma
text: Avoid demanding details, comparing their experience to another person’s, questioning why they acted a certain way, or promising that recovery will be quick. Reassurance should not minimize genuine danger. If you are a friend, teacher, caregiver or community volunteer, remain within your role and refer for professional care when needed.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Guided reflection: choose, do not disclose
text: This exercise deliberately does not ask you to describe a traumatic event. Skip any question that feels uncomfortable. You may reflect privately without writing anything down.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — A seven-day gentle support practice
text: This is not a treatment course or a promise that trauma symptoms will resolve in seven days. Any day can be repeated, replaced or skipped. For ongoing severe symptoms, seek qualified care rather than relying on the practice plan alone.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Publication and safeguarding review
text: Status: Evidence-informed material under editorial review. Not yet approved for clinical publication. Before release through VUGA NDAKUMVA, a licensed mental health professional should verify clinical wording, a safeguarding specialist should review emergency pathways, Rwanda-based partners should verify local support services, and expert translators should validate Kinyarwanda and French adaptations. Accessibility and user-comprehension checks are also required.

title: Understanding Trauma and Post-Traumatic Stress — Publication and safeguarding review
text: Editorial boundary: This material describes trauma and PTSD but never diagnoses an individual, provides unsupervised trauma processing, or supplies unverified emergency numbers. Case examples are fictional teaching illustrations.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — What grief means
text: Grief is the response people may have when someone or something important is lost. The loss may be the death of a loved one, the end of a relationship, leaving a familiar place, losing employment, a change in health, or the loss of an anticipated future. Responses can include sadness, longing, anger, guilt, relief, confusion, numbness, or even moments of happiness. None of these feelings alone defines how much the loss mattered.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — What grief means
text: Bereavement refers specifically to the experience of losing someone through death. Mourning is the way grief may be expressed within a family, culture, faith, or community, such as gatherings, remembrance, silence, or rituals. Adjustment means learning to live with changes that follow loss. Adjustment is not the same as forgetting or no longer caring. [1,2]

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Different types of loss
text: Death-related loss: A person may grieve a parent, partner, child, friend, colleague, or another important person. The relationship may have been loving, conflicted, distant, or complicated; each can produce genuine grief.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Different types of loss
text: Living losses: The end of a relationship, migration, infertility, disability, an illness diagnosis, job loss, separation from a community, or a major change in personal identity can bring grief-like responses. These experiences deserve support, although the clinical diagnosis of prolonged grief disorder applies specifically to bereavement following death.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Different types of loss
text: Anticipatory grief: Some people experience grief before a likely loss, such as when caring for a person with advanced illness. They may feel sadness and uncertainty while also hoping for improvement.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Different types of loss
text: Ambiguous loss: Some losses have no clear ending, such as the unexplained absence of a loved one or major changes in a family member’s memory or personality. Uncertainty may make emotional adjustment particularly difficult. These terms describe experiences, not automatic diagnoses.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Why everyone grieves differently
text: The meaning of the relationship, the circumstances of the loss, earlier experiences, physical health, family responsibilities, financial conditions, available support, and cultural expectations all affect grieving. One person may cry frequently; another may concentrate on practical tasks. Some seek company; others prefer periods of solitude. People may also move between these responses.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Why everyone grieves differently
text: There is no requirement to experience grief in a certain order. Popular descriptions of “stages” may be useful language for some people, but they are not a universal sequence or a checklist that everyone must complete. [1]

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Emotional responses to grief
text: Sadness and longing may arise when a place, song, routine, or anniversary reminds a person of the loss. Anger may be directed at the situation, an institution, other people, or oneself. Guilt may involve repeated thoughts such as “I should have known” or “I could have done more.” Fear may concern finances, parenting alone, future relationships, or losing others.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Emotional responses to grief
text: Feeling numb, relieved, or temporarily happy does not mean the person is uncaring. Relief may coexist with sadness, particularly after a long period of caregiving or suffering. People may need permission to hold several emotions at once without judging themselves.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — How grief can affect the body and daily life
text: Some bereaved people experience fatigue, interrupted sleep, appetite changes, headaches, muscle tension, difficulty concentrating, forgetfulness, low motivation, or reduced interest in social activities. Practical tasks can suddenly feel harder because attention and energy are limited.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — How grief can affect the body and daily life
text: Not every physical symptom is caused by grief. New, severe, or persistent medical symptoms should be assessed by a healthcare professional. Chest pain, significant breathing difficulty, fainting, or other emergency symptoms require urgent medical attention. [1]

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Grief over time: waves rather than a straight line
text: For many people, very intense feelings gradually become less constant, but reminders can bring renewed grief years later. A birthday, holiday, graduation, or family event may evoke sadness and affection together. Grief can change in character: a person may still miss someone deeply while becoming able to study, work, connect, and experience enjoyment.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Grief over time: waves rather than a straight line
text: The aim of adjustment is not to erase the relationship. A continuing sense of connection through memories, values, stories, and meaningful practices can coexist with taking part in present life. There is no deadline by which someone must “move on.”

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Grief, depression, and trauma: important distinctions
text: Grief often centres on the loss and reminders of it, with emotions that may rise and fall. Major depression may involve persistent low mood or loss of pleasure across many aspects of life, alongside other symptoms and impairment. PTSD may involve intrusive traumatic memories, avoidance, threat-related arousal, and other symptoms following traumatic exposure. These experiences can overlap; one person may require assessment for more than one condition.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Grief, depression, and trauma: important distinctions
text: Neither a short checklist nor the passage of a few weeks can establish a diagnosis. A professional evaluates the full pattern, medical factors, risk, functioning, and cultural context. [2,3]

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Prolonged grief disorder: when grief becomes severely impairing
text: A minority of bereaved people experience grief that remains unusually intense and pervasive, with strong yearning or preoccupation, substantial emotional pain, and major difficulty engaging in daily life. In prolonged grief disorder, the disturbance exceeds what is expected in the person’s cultural and social context and causes significant impairment.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Prolonged grief disorder: when grief becomes severely impairing
text: The WHO ICD-11 describes grief persisting for an atypically long period, with more than six months as a minimum. The DSM-5-TR requires at least twelve months for adults and six months for children and adolescents, plus additional clinical symptoms and impairment. These thresholds are not self-diagnosis rules. Someone experiencing severe distress can seek support before either threshold. [3,4]

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Healthy coping: meeting basic needs first
text: Grief can make ordinary routines seem demanding. Gentle attention to hydration, meals, rest, medication as prescribed, and safe physical movement may protect wellbeing. A person need not pursue a perfect routine. Small achievable steps, such as eating a meal or taking a brief walk, can be a reasonable beginning.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Healthy coping: meeting basic needs first
text: Try to avoid relying on alcohol, recreational drugs, or gambling to reduce grief-related pain. These may worsen mental health or create additional problems. If practical needs such as childcare, transport, paperwork, or finances are overwhelming, asking for concrete help can be as valuable as discussing feelings. [1,5]

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Coping with reminders, anniversaries, and memories
text: Reminders may arrive unexpectedly through photographs, songs, familiar places, smells, or conversations. If a reminder causes distress, a person may pause, notice their surroundings, and choose whether to continue, leave the situation, call someone, or rest. There is no obligation to view photos, keep particular belongings, or participate in rituals before feeling ready.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Coping with reminders, anniversaries, and memories
text: Anniversaries may be easier with a flexible plan: deciding how much company is wanted, arranging transport or a quiet space, choosing a meaningful activity if desired, and allowing plans to change. Some people prefer remembrance; others prefer ordinary routine. Both can be valid.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Social support and asking for help
text: A supportive relationship does not require another person to fix grief. It may involve a listening ear, sitting together, helping with meals, accompanying someone to an appointment, caring for children, or checking in without demanding a response. Support should be offered rather than imposed.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Social support and asking for help
text: People vary in whom they trust. Family, faith communities, peers, and community groups can be valuable when they respect privacy and consent, but no one should be pressured to disclose personal experiences or follow a particular mourning practice.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Supporting someone who is grieving
text: Start with simple, direct care: “I’m sorry this has happened. I can listen if you want, or help with something practical.” Let the person decide whether to talk. Avoid comparing losses, insisting that they be strong, interpreting their emotions, or giving fixed deadlines. Rather than saying “Let me know if you need anything,” offer a choice of specific assistance: preparing a meal, helping with transport, checking on household duties, or accompanying them to seek professional help. Follow through on promised support. [5]

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Children and adolescents experiencing grief
text: Children may express grief through play, questions, clinginess, irritability, sleep changes, withdrawal, or changes at school. A young child may ask repeatedly about the death as their understanding develops. Adolescents may want privacy while still needing dependable adult support.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Children and adolescents experiencing grief
text: Give age-appropriate, truthful explanations; avoid confusing euphemisms when children need to understand that a person has died. Keep routines where possible and identify a trusted adult who can answer questions. Do not insist that children participate in memorial activities or share feelings publicly. Persistent changes in safety, behavior, sleep, or school functioning warrant professional assessment. [5]

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Grief across families and cultures
text: Communities differ in funeral practices, periods of mourning, how emotions are expressed, and how responsibility is shared. Rwanda’s diverse family and community contexts may shape remembrance, practical support, and use of faith traditions. A respectful educational resource asks what is meaningful to the individual rather than prescribing one response.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Grief across families and cultures
text: Some people find comfort in prayer or religious communities; others do not. Spiritual support may complement healthcare when freely chosen. No person should be blamed for grief, excluded from support, or told that clinical care is unnecessary because of beliefs.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — When to seek professional support
text: Consider speaking with a qualified health or mental health professional when grief is severely overwhelming, interferes with essential activities, continues to worsen, includes persistent depression or traumatic stress symptoms, or is accompanied by harmful substance use. Help is appropriate even when the loss happened recently.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — When to seek professional support
text: A clinician can assess whether the person is experiencing a depressive disorder, PTSD, prolonged grief disorder, a physical health issue, or another concern, and discuss appropriate treatment and support. Some people benefit from structured grief-focused psychotherapy. Medication is not a universal treatment for grief itself; it may be considered for an independently diagnosed condition under professional guidance. [3,4,5]

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Safety and urgent help
text: Suicidal thoughts, intent to self-harm, inability to stay safe, severe confusion, or immediate threats to life require urgent help. Contact available local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department. If a person is in immediate danger, remain with them only when safe to do so and seek urgent assistance.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Safety and urgent help
text: If someone says they want to die, respond calmly and take the statement seriously. Do not argue, shame, or promise to keep imminent danger secret. Help connect them to qualified emergency or mental health care. The exact Rwanda referral numbers and facilities must be verified by VUGA NDAKUMVA before this chapter is published as a public-facing resource.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Reflection and assessment
text: Do not require learners to describe their own bereavement. They may answer using a fictional situation or choose not to participate.

title: Understanding Grief, Loss, and Emotional Adjustment — Evidence and professional review
text: Editorial status: Evidence-informed educational material; not yet clinically approved or authorized for public release.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — What is sleep, and why do we need it?
text: Sleep is a natural, recurring state in which the brain and body undergo coordinated changes. It is not simply a period of inactivity. During sleep, the brain cycles through different stages that support attention, learning, memory, emotional processing and physical functioning. The value of sleep is not measured by duration alone: timing, continuity and how rested a person feels during the day also matter. [1-3]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — What is sleep, and why do we need it?
text: A single difficult night is common and does not necessarily indicate a disorder. Sleep becomes a greater concern when problems persist, are distressing, or interfere with safe and effective daily life. A person with adequate time in bed may still get poor-quality sleep because of repeated awakenings or an underlying disorder.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — What is sleep, and why do we need it?
text: Sleep and mental health affect each other. Stress, anxiety, depression, trauma-related symptoms and other difficulties may interfere with sleep. Repeated poor sleep can also worsen concentration, irritability, emotional regulation and coping capacity. This does not mean that every person who sleeps poorly has a mental illness. [3,4]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — The body clock: circadian rhythm
text: The circadian rhythm is an approximately 24-hour timing system that influences when we feel alert, sleepy, hungry and ready for activity. Light, daily activity and regular waking patterns help synchronize it. The brain receives information about environmental light and uses it to coordinate the sleep-wake cycle. The hormone melatonin typically rises as darkness approaches, helping signal nighttime. [2]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — The body clock: circadian rhythm
text: For example, a student who stays awake on a phone until very late and sleeps until noon on weekends may find it difficult to become sleepy at an earlier school-night bedtime. However, teenagers naturally tend toward later sleep timing than younger children; this biological shift should not be mistaken for laziness.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — The body clock: circadian rhythm
text: A second process is the drive to sleep that builds while we are awake. Sleep pressure generally increases as waking hours pass and decreases during sleep. Together, sleep pressure and the circadian rhythm influence when we fall asleep and wake up. Caffeine can temporarily reduce our sense of sleepiness but does not replace the restorative functions of sleep. [2]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — What happens during the night?
text: Typical sleep contains both non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) and rapid-eye-movement (REM) stages, cycling several times. Patterns change with age and across the night. [5]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — What happens during the night?
text: No single stage is the only "important" stage. Normal sleep includes a balance across stages, and consumer sleep trackers cannot reliably diagnose a sleep disorder based solely on their stage estimates.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — How much sleep is generally recommended?
text: Recommended sleep amounts depend on age, and they describe population guidance rather than a rigid score for each individual. Some people need more sleep when ill or recovering from lost sleep. [1,6]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — How much sleep is generally recommended?
text: A person who works long shifts, shares a crowded home, experiences nighttime noise, or cares for a young child may have limited control over sleep time. Educational advice must acknowledge these real barriers instead of blaming the individual.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — What is insufficient or poor-quality sleep?
text: Insufficient sleep means obtaining less sleep than the body needs. Sleep deficiency can also involve poor timing, interrupted sleep, or a condition that reduces restorative sleep. Possible daytime consequences include low alertness, difficulty remembering information, slower reaction time, changes in mood and greater risk during driving or hazardous tasks. [3]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — What is insufficient or poor-quality sleep?
text: Symptoms can also arise from anemia, medication side effects, other illnesses, depression or other conditions. A professional assessment can help determine the cause.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Insomnia: more than one bad night
text: Insomnia involves difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or returning to sleep after waking, despite an adequate opportunity to sleep, with associated distress or daytime impairment. Temporary insomnia may follow stress, illness, travel, grief or major changes. Chronic insomnia is a more persistent clinical pattern and should not be diagnosed from a simple website checklist. [7-9]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Insomnia: more than one bad night
text: A person who worries about whether they will sleep may become increasingly alert at bedtime. Spending extra hours awake in bed, monitoring the clock, or irregular sleep timing can sometimes maintain the problem. Persistent insomnia may also coexist with pain, anxiety, depression, substance use or other sleep disorders.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Insomnia: more than one bad night
text: Example: A university student spends several nights awake before examinations. After the examination ends, the student keeps worrying about sleep and begins staying in bed much longer to "catch up." The difficulty continues. A clinician can assess whether insomnia-focused treatment is appropriate.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Other sleep conditions people should know about
text: Sleep apnea may involve repeated breathing interruptions, loud snoring, gasping or choking during sleep, and daytime sleepiness. Not everyone with sleep apnea snores. People with these symptoms should seek medical assessment; sleep hygiene alone cannot treat the underlying breathing disorder.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Other sleep conditions people should know about
text: Some people cannot align their natural sleep timing with work, school or social schedules. Shift work, jet lag and delayed sleep timing may contribute. Treatment depends on the pattern and may require specialist guidance.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Other sleep conditions people should know about
text: Uncomfortable sensations that improve with moving the legs, unusual behaviors during sleep, or severe daytime sleepiness deserve evaluation. Falling asleep unexpectedly or experiencing sleep attacks should not be assumed to result only from a busy schedule.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — How sleep and mental health interact
text: When the body is on alert, it can be harder to settle at night. Sleep loss can make daily stressors feel harder to manage. Gentle routines may help, but people facing ongoing insecurity or hardship also need practical support.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — How sleep and mental health interact
text: Worry about future events or sleep itself may prolong wakefulness. Persistent sleep difficulties and anxiety symptoms should be assessed together rather than treated as unrelated issues.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — How sleep and mental health interact
text: Depression may be associated with difficulty sleeping, early waking or sleeping much longer than usual. Changes in sleep alone do not establish depression, and treatment decisions require careful assessment.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — How sleep and mental health interact
text: Nightmares, hypervigilance or a feeling of unsafety may disrupt rest. Survivors should not be pressured to close their eyes, disclose memories, or perform relaxation exercises that increase distress.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — How sleep and mental health interact
text: A markedly reduced need for sleep accompanied by unusually high energy, elevated or irritable mood, racing thoughts or impulsive behavior can be a warning sign that needs prompt professional assessment. This is different from ordinary insomnia accompanied by fatigue.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Everyday habits that can support sleep
text: Healthy sleep routines are useful for general wellbeing and can complement clinical care. They are not, on their own, an adequate treatment for chronic insomnia disorder. [1,8-10]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Practical barriers in Rwanda-relevant daily life
text: A reader may share one room with family members, work evening shifts, study under difficult conditions, manage caregiving duties or have limited privacy. Advice should prioritize realistic actions. For example, a household may coordinate a quieter period, reduce unnecessary night lighting, or plan a more reliable morning routine when possible. These are illustrative situations, not claims about all Rwandan households.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Practical barriers in Rwanda-relevant daily life
text: When poverty, housing insecurity, severe stress, violence or illness disrupt sleep, an individual routine cannot resolve the underlying problem. Health education should connect people to medical, social and practical support where appropriate.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Evidence-based care for persistent insomnia
text: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured treatment that addresses sleep-related patterns of thinking and behavior. It can include education, tailored behavioral strategies, cognitive approaches and follow-up. Multiple clinical guidelines recommend multicomponent CBT-I as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults. [8,9]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Evidence-based care for persistent insomnia
text: Specialist CBT-I may include methods such as sleep restriction or sleep compression. These should not be copied from a handout without assessment, especially for people with certain medical or psychiatric conditions, excessive daytime sleepiness, high-risk work, or complex sleep problems.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Evidence-based care for persistent insomnia
text: A clinician may consider medication depending on symptoms, age, other conditions, pregnancy status, interactions and treatment history. Sleeping pills can have side effects and may not address the underlying cause. Do not start, combine, stop or change prescribed medicines on the basis of this chapter. Melatonin is not a universal cure for insomnia and suitability varies. [7,10]

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — When should someone seek professional help?
text: Consider an appointment with a qualified healthcare professional when sleep difficulty persists, significantly affects mood, concentration, study or work, or occurs alongside loud snoring, breathing interruptions, repeated nightmares, unusual movements, severe daytime sleepiness, chronic pain or symptoms of a mental health condition.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — When should someone seek professional help?
text: Urgent medical assessment is warranted if a person has severe or unusual breathing problems, episodes of losing consciousness, serious injury associated with sleepiness, or new concerning symptoms. If a person is dangerously sleepy, they should not drive or operate machinery. If there are thoughts of suicide or immediate danger, seek urgent emergency assistance through available local emergency services or the nearest emergency department.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — When should someone seek professional help?
text: Where symptoms suggest mania or a significantly reduced need for sleep with marked behavioral changes, seek prompt clinical assessment.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Guided activity A - My seven-day sleep observation
text: For seven days, readers may record sleep patterns without trying to force a target. This exercise is for awareness, not diagnosis or clinical sleep restriction. Avoid recording sensitive details on devices that are shared or monitored.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Guided activity A - My seven-day sleep observation
text: After the week, consider whether patterns change with shift work, phone use, stress, noise, illness, caffeine or caregiving. Bring the notes to a clinician if a sleep problem is ongoing. If recording sleep increases anxiety, stop tracking.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Guided activity B - A gentle evening routine
text: Choose one or two realistic steps, not a rigid checklist: (1) identify tomorrow's priority tasks earlier in the evening, (2) choose a quiet activity for the final part of the day, (3) adjust brightness or noise where feasible, and (4) allow yourself to rest without checking the clock repeatedly.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Guided activity B - A gentle evening routine
text: Reflection: Which step is feasible in your home? What barrier would require someone else's cooperation? A routine should be adapted to safety, disability, caregiving and work schedules.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Guided activity C - Distinguishing a worry from a plan
text: Write down an ordinary concern earlier in the evening if doing so feels comfortable. Divide it into "something I can act on tomorrow" and "something I cannot solve tonight." Choose one practical next action for tomorrow. Do not use this exercise to dismiss real danger, pain or urgent needs.

title: Understanding Sleep and Mental Wellbeing — Guided activity C - Distinguishing a worry from a plan
text: Example: "I may be late for work" can become "I will prepare my bag and check my transport plan." If a concern involves an unsafe environment or a serious medical symptom, practical safety assistance takes priority over relaxation.

text: Circadian rhythm: An approximately 24-hour cycle regulating alertness and many bodily functions.
