title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Why relationships matter for mental health
text: People develop and maintain wellbeing through many forms of connection: friendships, family ties, classmates, colleagues, neighbours, mentors, peers, and chosen communities. Supportive relationships may offer comfort during setbacks, practical assistance, recognition, shared enjoyment, and a sense of belonging. They are one among many influences on mental health, alongside biology, life experiences, economic security, and access to healthcare [1-3].

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Why relationships matter for mental health
text: Social connection is not measured only by the number of people in someone’s contacts. A person may have many acquaintances but few relationships in which they feel safe and understood. Another person may have a small circle and feel well supported. Relationship quality, reliability, and personal choice matter.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Why relationships matter for mental health
text: Connection can protect wellbeing without guaranteeing that a person will never experience depression, anxiety, or another mental health condition. Similarly, being socially isolated does not prove someone has a disorder. [1-3]

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Understanding social connection, loneliness, isolation, and solitude
text: Social connection describes the structure, functions, and quality of how people relate to others. Structure includes who is in a person’s network and how often they interact. Function includes the type of emotional or practical support exchanged. Quality concerns whether interactions feel supportive, trustworthy, strained, or harmful. This three-part explanation follows the WHO social-connection framework [1].

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Understanding social connection, loneliness, isolation, and solitude
text: Loneliness is a distressing feeling that occurs when a person experiences a gap between the relationships they want and those they believe they have. A person can feel lonely in a crowded classroom, busy workplace, or household. Loneliness is not a character flaw or proof of unpopularity

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Understanding social connection, loneliness, isolation, and solitude
text: Social isolation refers to having relatively few relationships, social roles, or interactions. It may result from geographic distance, disability-related barriers, bereavement, discrimination, relocation, low income, or other circumstances. Someone can be isolated without feeling lonely, although the two often overlap [1].

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Understanding social connection, loneliness, isolation, and solitude
text: Solitude is time spent alone, sometimes intentionally and comfortably. Quiet time for rest, prayer, creative work, or reflection can be valuable. Being alone is not automatically unhealthy. What matters is whether the person can access the level and quality of connection they need.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Understanding social connection, loneliness, isolation, and solitude
text: Which word best describes your current experience: connected, lonely, isolated, enjoying solitude, or unsure? There is no right answer. You may experience more than one at the same time.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Healthy relationships: what to look for
text: A healthy relationship is not a relationship without disagreements. It is one in which people can disagree, grow, and make choices while preserving one another’s dignity. Healthy relationships may include:

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Healthy relationships: what to look for
text: Family, friendship, romantic, and professional relationships have different expectations. The same principle applies across them: caring for someone does not authorize monitoring, humiliating, isolating, or coercing them.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Social support: emotional, practical, informational, and belonging
text: People need different kinds of support at different times. Emotional support involves empathy and being listened to. Practical support may include help with transportation, childcare, or sharing a task. Informational support involves reliable guidance or help finding services. Belonging comes from being part of a group in which a person feels accepted [2,3].

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Social support: emotional, practical, informational, and belonging
text: A student worried about examinations may benefit from a peer who listens, a tutor who helps organise revision, and a trusted adult who notices exhaustion. No single person has to meet all those needs. Developing more than one safe connection can reduce dependence on an individual relationship.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Social support: emotional, practical, informational, and belonging
text: Offering support should not become pressure. Ask what someone wants before giving advice, involving others, or sharing a private situation.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Why making and maintaining connections can be difficult
text: Challenges such as moving to a new district, unemployment, heavy school workloads, disability-related access barriers, caregiving, bereavement, social anxiety, experiences of discrimination, or limited money for transport can make maintaining relationships difficult. This is not evidence that a person is unwilling or incapable of friendship.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Why making and maintaining connections can be difficult
text: Some people also need more time alone than others. The goal is not to force sociability or make everyone attend large gatherings. It is to support meaningful relationships that fit individual preferences and safety.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Why making and maintaining connections can be difficult
text: When a person has been hurt or controlled in a relationship, rebuilding trust may require time and professional support. Encouraging immediate reconnection with unsafe individuals can increase risk.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Listening and communicating with care
text: Communication is not just about speaking clearly. It also involves checking what someone means, allowing silence, and noticing whether the conversation feels safe. Helpful skills can be practised gradually.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Listening and communicating with care
text: An “I” statement can make concerns easier to discuss, but it is not a guaranteed way to resolve conflict. If the other person threatens or intimidates you, communication techniques are not a substitute for safety planning.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Listening and communicating with care
text: Active listening involves giving attention, avoiding unnecessary interruption, reflecting the meaning of what someone says, and asking permission before offering advice. A supportive reply may sound like: “That sounds exhausting. Would you prefer that I listen or help you think about options?”

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Interpersonal conflict and healthy repair
text: Disagreements can arise from expectations, stress, financial strain, misunderstandings, or different priorities. Constructive conflict management includes slowing down, focusing on a specific issue, allowing each person a voice, agreeing on a realistic next step, and revisiting the matter when calm.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Interpersonal conflict and healthy repair
text: For instance, two housemates may disagree over shared chores. They could identify the tasks, discuss what each can realistically manage, write down a fair arrangement, and review it after a week. The goal is not winning an argument but developing a workable agreement.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Interpersonal conflict and healthy repair
text: Ordinary disagreement is not the same as intimidation, coercive control, stalking, threats, or violence. If a person feels unsafe, avoid encouraging joint confrontation, mediation, or couples exercises as a default. Seek appropriate specialist assistance instead.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Emotional boundaries and personal autonomy
text: Boundaries are limits that protect time, privacy, emotional energy, and personal choices. A boundary is not a punishment; it describes what a person can accept and what they will do to care for themselves. Examples include choosing when to answer messages, deciding what information to share, asking before discussing a sensitive topic, and refusing to lend money one cannot afford to lose.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Emotional boundaries and personal autonomy
text: A respectful boundary might be: “I cannot talk about this during work. I can speak after 6 p.m.”

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Emotional boundaries and personal autonomy
text: Another might be: “I am not ready to discuss that experience.” Setting a boundary does not guarantee another person will respect it. In unsafe relationships, personal safety should take priority over explaining a boundary repeatedly.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Emotional boundaries and personal autonomy
text: Emotional support does not mean becoming someone’s clinician, remaining available every hour, or keeping dangerous secrets. It is appropriate to seek extra help when a problem exceeds what a friend or family member can safely manage.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Loneliness and its effects on wellbeing
text: Prolonged loneliness and isolation are associated with poorer mental and physical health, although the relationship is complex and not all individuals are affected in the same way [1-4]. Loneliness may involve sadness, restlessness, reduced motivation, difficulty trusting others, or the sense that one is disconnected even while surrounded by people.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Loneliness and its effects on wellbeing
text: Noticing loneliness can be a useful signal that a need for connection is unmet. It should not be treated as a diagnosis. A person whose loneliness occurs alongside persistent low mood, anxiety, sleep disturbance, or substantial impairment may benefit from professional assessment.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Digital relationships and online wellbeing
text: Messaging apps, online learning groups, and social platforms can help people stay connected across long distances. They can also create pressure to respond immediately, comparisons with others, misunderstandings, or exposure to harassment. The quality and safety of an interaction matter more than whether it happens online or in person.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Digital relationships and online wellbeing
text: Useful digital boundaries include asking before sharing someone else’s photo or story, respecting delayed replies, choosing privacy settings thoughtfully, and avoiding arguments in public comment sections when a private conversation would be safer. Digital access may not be private for someone whose device is monitored. If someone is being threatened or monitored, changing settings or blocking a contact might alert the person causing harm. Specialist digital safety support may be needed before taking action.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Families, friends, peers, and caregivers
text: Families and caregivers can support wellbeing through reliable attention, predictable care, encouragement, and help during difficulties. Friends and peers may provide acceptance and shared experiences. Teachers, mentors, health workers, and community members may also become valuable sources of support.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Families, friends, peers, and caregivers
text: However, not every family or community relationship is safe. People should not be encouraged to disclose private mental health concerns to relatives, religious leaders, or peers without considering trust, confidentiality, and personal choice.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Families, friends, peers, and caregivers
text: For adolescents, safe relationships with trusted adults are important. Adults should listen respectfully, avoid dismissing concerns as “just a phase,” and seek appropriate professional or safeguarding assistance when serious risks arise [3,5].

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Community belonging in Rwanda
text: In Rwanda, possible opportunities for social connection may include school clubs, youth groups, sports teams, community activities, volunteer initiatives, faith communities, study circles, neighbourhood associations, and peer-support programmes. These are illustrative settings, not guaranteed services or endorsements.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Community belonging in Rwanda
text: Participation should remain voluntary. Activities should be inclusive of people with disabilities, individuals living far from community centres, people with limited connectivity, and those who may not feel safe in some groups. Privacy and protection from stigma are especially important when mental health is discussed.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Community belonging in Rwanda
text: Community programmes can support connection by providing accessible meeting places, predictable schedules, welcoming facilitators, and a way to raise concerns safely [1,2].

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Supporting someone who feels lonely or distressed
text: Begin by asking how the person would like to be supported. Offer specific, practical options instead of making broad promises. For example: “Would you like me to check in this weekend?” or “Would it help to walk together after class?” Respect a no and avoid turning an invitation into pressure.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Supporting someone who feels lonely or distressed
text: Do not assume that frequent contact is always best. Some people need time, rest, or privacy. If a person speaks about hopelessness, self-harm, or suicide, take it seriously and seek appropriate urgent professional support. Do not promise to keep an immediate safety risk secret.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — When professional support is appropriate
text: Consider consultation with a qualified healthcare or mental health professional when loneliness, social withdrawal, or interpersonal stress becomes persistent, overwhelming, or interferes with sleep, school, employment, or daily responsibilities; when anxiety or depression symptoms are present; or when repeated conflict or trauma makes it difficult to feel safe.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — When professional support is appropriate
text: Urgent assistance is needed when there is immediate danger, threats of serious violence, or concern that someone may act on thoughts of suicide or self-harm. Seek available emergency medical assistance or the nearest appropriate emergency facility. Specific Rwanda contacts and operating hours must be confirmed before publication of this chapter.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Glossary
text: Social connection: Relationships and interactions considered in terms of structure, support function, and quality.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Glossary
text: Loneliness: Distress caused by a perceived gap between desired and existing connections.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Glossary
text: Social isolation: Relatively few social relationships or interactions.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Glossary
text: Emotional boundary: A limit around emotional availability, disclosure, or personal responsibility.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Glossary
text: Active listening: Attentive, respectful listening aimed at understanding rather than immediately judging or fixing.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Glossary
text: Coercive control: A pattern of intimidation or restrictions used to dominate another person.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Glossary
text: Belonging: Feeling accepted and valued as part of a relationship or group.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — References and evidence notes
text: Evidence note: The chapter paraphrases official source guidance and adds original, fictional scenarios and educational exercises. These exercises are practical teaching examples; they have not been independently tested as a clinical intervention. No local referral contact is asserted as verified in this version.

title: Relationships, Social Connection, and Mental Wellbeing — Publication review checklist
text: Before public release: (1) clinical review; (2) safeguarding and domestic-violence safety review; (3) fact-check of references and Rwanda-specific services; (4) plain-language and accessibility review; (5) culturally appropriate Kinyarwanda/French translations; (6) version control and scheduled review date.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — What does child and adolescent mental health mean?
text: Child mental health includes emotional wellbeing, developing skills to manage feelings, building friendships, learning, and participating in family and school life. Having good mental health does not mean a child is calm or happy every day. Children may feel frustrated, frightened, angry, or sad while still growing in healthy ways. [R1, R2]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — What does child and adolescent mental health mean?
text: Adolescence commonly refers to ages 10–19. It brings rapid physical, cognitive and social changes. Young people increasingly seek autonomy, explore identity, become sensitive to peer relationships and manage growing responsibilities. These changes are important, but they do not always happen at the same speed. [R1]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — What does child and adolescent mental health mean?
text: The World Health Organization estimated in 2025 that approximately one in seven adolescents aged 10–19 lives with a mental health condition worldwide. This is a global estimate—not a Rwanda-specific prevalence figure—and shows why accessible, non-stigmatizing support matters.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Emotional development across life stages
text: Younger children often communicate distress through behaviour, play, sleep, appetite or physical complaints before they can describe complex feelings. They need adults who help name emotions, keep predictable routines and model calm responses. This does not mean every tantrum or fear is a mental illness.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Emotional development across life stages
text: School-age children usually develop more complex friendships and a growing sense of fairness, achievement and belonging. Academic pressure, conflicts, exclusion, family changes and difficulties with learning can affect mood and confidence. Adults can support them by listening and responding with consistent, fair boundaries.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Emotional development across life stages
text: Adolescents may want privacy, independence and greater control over decisions. Respectful family relationships balance this growing autonomy with appropriate safeguarding. A change in interests or desire for time alone can be normal; a persistent decline in functioning or safety requires attention. [R1, R2]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Risk and protective factors
text: A child’s mental health is shaped by interacting biological, psychological and social factors. Family instability, discrimination, food insecurity, chronic illness, harmful punishment, abuse, bullying, isolation or major loss can increase risk. These experiences do not guarantee a disorder, and no single factor explains an individual child’s difficulties. [R1, R3]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Risk and protective factors
text: Protective factors include caring, dependable adults; safe learning environments; accessible healthcare; friends and community support; opportunities for play and activity; respectful discipline; and skills such as problem-solving and emotional regulation. Protection is a shared responsibility, not a task for the child alone. [R3, R4]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Common mental health challenges
text: Anxiety and fear: Children may experience persistent worries, fear of separation, social situations or particular events. When fear is intense, prolonged, and interferes with attendance, sleep, relationships or daily activities, assessment may help.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Common mental health challenges
text: Depression and low mood: Signs may include sustained sadness or irritability, reduced interest, hopelessness, withdrawal or changes in energy and sleep. Irritability in adolescents can be prominent; it should not simply be dismissed as “bad behaviour.”

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Common mental health challenges
text: Attention, behaviour and learning: Persistent attention difficulties, impulsivity, aggression, or school struggles can have different explanations, including neurodevelopmental needs, learning barriers, stress, trauma or sleep problems. Effective responses begin with careful assessment, not punishment.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Common mental health challenges
text: Trauma, eating concerns and substance use: Some young people experience distress after frightening events, changes in eating or body image, or harmful use of substances. Each deserves sensitive, age-appropriate support and clinical evaluation when needed. [R1, R2]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — What is a warning sign rather than a normal phase?
text: A single bad day, argument or lower grade usually does not establish a mental health condition. Pay attention to duration, intensity, change from the child’s usual behaviour, distress and impact on daily life. Persistent school refusal, marked withdrawal, severe sleep changes, repeated unexplained physical complaints, loss of enjoyable activities or significant impairment merit a supportive conversation and possible assessment.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — What is a warning sign rather than a normal phase?
text: Watch urgently for expressed wishes to die, suicidal behaviour, self-injury, extreme confusion, psychotic symptoms, immediate danger, severe inability to care for basic needs, or signs of abuse. Never wait for a routine appointment if danger appears imminent. [R1, R2]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — What is a warning sign rather than a normal phase?
text: Do not label or diagnose: “This child has depression” or “This teenager has ADHD” should not follow from a web checklist. Document observations without judgement and consult an appropriately qualified clinician.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — School experience and mental wellbeing
text: School can be a powerful place of belonging, but also a source of distress. Examinations, performance expectations, classroom humiliation, learning differences, peer exclusion and disciplinary practices can influence emotions and participation. Educators can improve wellbeing by building predictable routines, demonstrating fairness, welcoming differences and providing ways to ask for help.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — School experience and mental wellbeing
text: When a learner struggles, private and respectful inquiry is preferable to public embarrassment. Teachers should record observable changes, involve safeguarding or student-support staff according to school procedures, work with caregivers where safe and appropriate, and help families access professional assessment when indicated. [R4]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Bullying, exclusion and cyberbullying
text: Bullying generally involves repeated aggression and a power imbalance; it may involve physical acts, insults, humiliation, exclusion, threats or online abuse. Even a single serious incident can require protection. Adults should take reports seriously, make a proportionate safety plan, avoid blaming the affected child, and investigate according to safeguarding procedures.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Bullying, exclusion and cyberbullying
text: Online spaces may expose young people to harassment, unwanted sharing of private information, image-based abuse or coercion. Do not require a child to confront an aggressor. Before blocking accounts, collecting screenshots or altering devices, consider whether a harmful person monitors the child’s device and whether a safer adult or professional should assist. [R1, R4]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Supportive parenting and caregiving
text: Children benefit from warmth and consistent boundaries. Caregivers can listen first, acknowledge feelings, explain expectations without threats, offer manageable choices and repair relationships after conflict. “You seem quieter recently; would you like to tell me what has been difficult?” is more inviting than an accusation.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Supportive parenting and caregiving
text: Caregivers should avoid calling children weak, lazy or attention-seeking because of emotional difficulties. Encourage regular sleep opportunities, balanced meals where possible, play, movement, trusted friendships and reasonable schedules without making lifestyle changes the only response to a serious problem.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Supportive parenting and caregiving
text: If a parent or caregiver is the source of harm, the child needs an alternative safe adult and the appropriate safeguarding route—not forced family reconciliation. [R3, R4]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Communication that helps young people speak
text: Choose a private, calm time. Use open questions, listen without interrupting and reflect what you hear. The goal is not to extract a complete story immediately. Ask what feels safest or most helpful right now. A child can decline to answer an optional educational question, and a teenager’s privacy deserves respect within child-protection responsibilities.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Communication that helps young people speak
text: Adults should explain confidentiality honestly: they will respect privacy as much as possible, but may need to involve safeguarding or emergency services if someone is in danger or law requires action. Do not promise to keep abuse or immediate danger secret. [R4, R6]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Helping a young person experiencing distress
text: First check immediate safety and basic needs. Offer calm company and validate feelings without assuming a diagnosis. Ask whether they would prefer a different trusted adult, school staff member or health professional. Make a small plan together: who to contact, a suitable time and place, and how to manage school or home demands while support is arranged.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Helping a young person experiencing distress
text: When a child discloses violence or exploitation, do not question them repeatedly, demand evidence, suggest blame or confront the suspected person. Follow child safeguarding procedures and involve trained professionals. The child’s safety and developmental needs take priority. [R4, R6]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Mental health in digitally connected lives
text: Digital experiences can support friendship, learning and peer connection, but may also involve social comparison, disrupted sleep, unwanted contact, harassment or exposure to distressing content. Ask what the young person experiences online instead of assuming all screen time has the same effects. Agree on age-appropriate privacy, bedtime and safety practices. Adults should model respectful online behaviour and avoid secretive surveillance when a collaborative, safer approach is possible. If there is a credible threat, exploitation or urgent safety risk, safeguarding needs may override ordinary privacy expectations.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Supporting diverse needs and inclusion
text: Children with disabilities, neurodevelopmental differences, chronic illnesses, learning difficulties, displacement histories or experiences of discrimination may face additional barriers to care. Avoid assuming that all distress reflects an existing diagnosis or disability.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Supporting diverse needs and inclusion
text: Adapt communication by offering simple language, visual supports, extra response time, private alternatives to public sharing, and an accessible route to care. Ask families and young people what accommodations work for them. [R1, R2]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Evidence-based care and professional assessment
text: A clinician may speak with the child, caregivers and relevant educators, with appropriate privacy and consent procedures, to understand symptoms, context, functioning, medical history and safety concerns. Care may involve psychological interventions, family support, school adjustments, targeted services or medication when clinically indicated.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Evidence-based care and professional assessment
text: WHO recommends evidence-informed psychosocial interventions that build social-emotional skills and prevent mental health problems among adolescents. These are not substitutes for clinical treatment when a condition requires it. Do not recommend medicines, stop existing treatment or conduct trauma-processing therapies through self-help content. [R3]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — When and how to seek help in Rwanda
text: For non-emergency concerns, start with a qualified health professional, appropriate local health centre or hospital, and ask about child or adolescent mental health referral options. The Ministry of Health’s Kigali Mental Health Referral Centre publicly lists child and adolescent services; its published contact numbers are +250 793 902 059 and +250 736 440 666. Check current hours, service eligibility and referral arrangements before relying on them. [R7]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — When and how to seek help in Rwanda
text: For immediate danger or imminent self-harm risk, seek urgent medical or emergency assistance. Rwanda’s government emergency directory lists 112 for emergency assistance, 912 for ambulance and 116 for its child helpline. These are published numbers, not a guarantee that each line is staffed or suitable for every case at every moment. [R5]

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Short glossary
text: Mental wellbeing: The emotional, psychological and social functioning that supports daily life.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Short glossary
text: Co-regulation: An adult helping a child manage overwhelming emotions through calm, attuned support.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Short glossary
text: Protective factor: A condition or resource associated with safer development and resilience.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Short glossary
text: Safeguarding: Actions to protect children from harm and respond appropriately to safety concerns.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Short glossary
text: Psychosocial intervention: Structured support addressing thoughts, behaviour, relationships or social circumstances.

title: Child and Adolescent Mental Health — Short glossary
text: Referral: Connecting someone to a service qualified to assess or provide needed support.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — What gender-based violence means
text: Gender-based violence refers to harmful acts against a person that are connected to socially constructed gender differences, expectations, discrimination or unequal power. These acts can involve force, threats, intimidation, manipulation, coercion and restrictions on freedom. GBV can occur in intimate relationships, households, schools, workplaces, communities, institutions, humanitarian settings and online. [1,2]

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — What gender-based violence means
text: The term gender-based matters: it describes the relationship between violence and gender norms or power. Not every instance of interpersonal conflict is GBV. For example, two classmates disagreeing about a group project is not, by itself, GBV. But threatening a person because they reject an assigned gender role, or controlling a partner using gendered expectations of obedience, may be GBV.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Why GBV is a public health and human rights concern
text: GBV can undermine safety, bodily autonomy, health, education, employment, family relationships and participation in community life. The effects may persist after the violence ends. WHO describes violence against women as both a major public health and human rights problem. [1]

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Why GBV is a public health and human rights concern
text: WHO estimates published for 2023 indicate that approximately 840 million women and girls worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence from an intimate partner, or sexual violence by a non-partner, during their lifetime. This statistic describes a specific measured set of violence types; it does not measure every form of GBV or imply that all people share the same risk. [1]

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Why GBV is a public health and human rights concern
text: Figures should never be used to predict the experience of a particular person, to discredit a person whose experience differs from the average, or to claim that violence occurs equally in every community.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — What forms can GBV take?
text: Physical violence involves actions that inflict or threaten physical harm, such as hitting, pushing, restraining or threatening an assault. Threats can create fear even when no physical injury occurs. A person facing injury or an immediate threat needs safe, timely assistance.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — What forms can GBV take?
text: Sexual violence involves sexual acts or contact without free agreement, including through force, threats, intimidation, exploitation or inability to consent. Sexual violence can occur within marriage or an intimate partnership. A person may freeze or comply under fear; this does not establish consent. Prompt medical care can address injuries and time-sensitive health needs. [1,3]

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — What forms can GBV take?
text: Examples include repeated humiliation, serious threats, intimidation, deliberate isolation, constant surveillance or manipulation that undermines a person's autonomy. One rude remark does not automatically establish a pattern of abuse; context, frequency, intent and impact must be considered. A person does not need to prove a pattern before seeking help.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — What forms can GBV take?
text: Economic abuse occurs when access to income, work, property, essential resources or financial decisions is controlled to restrict another person's independence. Examples include preventing a partner from working or taking earnings through intimidation. Shared budgeting by mutual agreement is different from coercive financial control.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — What forms can GBV take?
text: This may include repeated unwanted monitoring, threats to publish private information, tracking without agreement, harassment using digital platforms or using access to a device to control another person. Digital safety choices should be tailored to the situation: abruptly changing passwords or deleting applications can sometimes alert an abusive person and increase risk.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — What forms can GBV take?
text: Children and adolescents can experience sexual exploitation, forced relationships, coercive control and other gender-related harm. Involving a trusted qualified child-protection service is essential when a child may be at risk. Adults should not promise unlimited secrecy; reporting duties and safeguarding processes can differ by case and jurisdiction.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Gender norms, inequality and unequal power
text: Gender norms are social ideas about how people are expected to behave because of gender. Some norms are harmless; others can promote entitlement, silence, inequality or tolerance of abuse. GBV risk can increase where harmful norms are reinforced by institutions, relationships or communities. [1,2]

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Gender norms, inequality and unequal power
text: Power does not come only from physical strength. A person may have control over money, housing, immigration or school status, employment, social reputation, childcare, or access to healthcare. When this power is used to threaten or restrict someone, the affected person may feel that resistance or disclosure is unsafe.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Gender norms, inequality and unequal power
text: Risk factors are not excuses. Alcohol use, financial strain, conflict or trauma history may be associated with violence in some settings, but responsibility for abusive actions belongs to the person who commits them.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Recognizing coercive control
text: Coercive control describes behaviors that may accumulate into a system of domination and fear. Examples include isolating a person from support, regulating movement, controlling access to money, intimidating children or pets, and repeatedly checking private communications. Individual signs do not establish a legal finding, but they deserve attention when they create fear or limit freedom.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Recognizing coercive control
text: A caring partner can express concern and discuss safety while respecting decisions. Control is more likely when one person uses fear, punishment, coercion, threats or surveillance to override the other person's choices. A person may experience both affection and abuse in the same relationship; affection does not cancel harmful behavior.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Effects on health, relationships and opportunity
text: GBV can have physical, sexual and reproductive, emotional, social and economic consequences. Not every survivor experiences all of them, and a person may show few outward signs. The absence of visible distress does not mean nothing happened. [1,3]

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Effects on health, relationships and opportunity
text: Injury, pain, sleep disturbance and some sexual or reproductive health concerns may arise. A medical professional can evaluate health needs and discuss options confidentially within applicable limits.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Effects on health, relationships and opportunity
text: Fear, anxiety, sadness, shame, emotional numbness, confusion, traumatic stress or difficulties trusting others may occur. Responses vary; feeling calm, detached or uncertain does not disprove abuse. Professional mental health support can be useful when difficulties persist or are severe.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Effects on health, relationships and opportunity
text: A survivor may lose income, miss classes, experience disruption to family relationships, avoid community activities, or find it difficult to use online services safely. Some effects are caused by threats or by lack of safe access to resources, not by a lack of resilience.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Why seeking help can be difficult
text: Reasons for delaying disclosure or remaining in a harmful situation may include fear of retaliation, financial dependence, threats involving children, stigma, attachment to the abusive person, uncertain legal outcomes, disability-related barriers, limited transport, fear of not being believed or concern about breaches of privacy.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Why seeking help can be difficult
text: Asking "Why didn't you leave?" often shifts attention away from the person causing harm. A more helpful question is "What would help you feel safer, and what choices are available to you?"

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Why seeking help can be difficult
text: A person may share only part of their experience, change their mind, or choose not to share details. Do not interrogate them, demand evidence, contact the person accused, or make a public disclosure on their behalf. The supporter's role is to listen, offer options and understand the limits of their own expertise.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Consent, choice and boundaries
text: Consent is a free and informed agreement to a specific action. It must not be obtained through threats, pressure, fear or exploitation. Consent can be withdrawn, and agreement to one action is not permission for another. Age, capacity and legal protections also matter, especially for children and people unable to consent.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Consent, choice and boundaries
text: Boundaries can concern physical contact, personal information, money, movement and digital devices. A boundary can be communicated in different ways. Silence or lack of resistance should not be automatically interpreted as agreement, especially when someone feels afraid.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Consent, choice and boundaries
text: Respectful: "I am worried about getting home safely. Would you like us to agree on a check-in?" Coercive: "Give me your password or I will punish you and stop paying for your transport."

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Consent, choice and boundaries
text: The difference includes freedom to decline without retaliation. Context and safety always matter.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Survivor-centred first-line support
text: The survivor-centred approach prioritizes safety, confidentiality (with explained limits), respect and non-discrimination. WHO's clinical handbook describes attention to immediate emotional, physical and safety needs as well as ongoing support. [3,4]

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Survivor-centred first-line support
text: This is a plain-language outline of the WHO LIVES first-line support approach. It is not a replacement for professional training. [3]

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Safety planning without increasing danger
text: Safety planning is an individualized conversation about possible risks, safe contacts and options. There is no one plan that works for everyone, and the person most affected often understands important risks that others cannot see. A trained specialist can help with higher-risk situations. [3,4]

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Safety planning without increasing danger
text: Important: Leaving an abusive relationship, changing device access or making a report can sometimes increase danger. General educational material should not direct everyone to take the same steps. It is safer to connect the person with a trained GBV service when possible.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Accessing support in Rwanda
text: Rwanda's Isange One Stop Centre model coordinates health, psychosocial, legal and other support for people affected by GBV. MIGEPROF describes an integrated package that can include safe shelter where required. [5] UNHCR Rwanda lists the Isange One Stop Centre toll-free contact as 3029 and states that services are available across Rwanda's 30 districts. UNHCR also notes that contacting an Isange Centre may involve reporting to law enforcement. People considering a referral should be informed of this possibility and ask about privacy and reporting procedures. [6]

text: 2026. VUGA NDAKUMVA must verify current operations, availability, eligibility and safe referral practices before publication, especially for urgent cases. Do not assume that every facility has identical hours or pathways.

title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence — Accessing support in Rwanda
text: After sexual assault, serious injury or a threat to immediate safety, prompt professional medical assessment is important. Some interventions are time-sensitive, and a clinician can explain available choices. The person should not be required to wait for a handbook activity or finish a questionnaire before seeking care. [3]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Understanding what counts as GBV
text: Gender-based violence refers to harmful actions directed against people because of gender or unequal gender-related power relations. It can occur in private and public, in person and through technology. It includes physical, sexual, psychological and economic harm, threats, coercion, and deprivation of liberty. Women and girls experience GBV disproportionately, while people of any gender may be affected. [1-3]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Understanding what counts as GBV
text: The word form describes how abuse is carried out - for example, a threat, an unwanted sexual act, or withholding money as a means of control. The word setting describes where or in which relationship it occurs - for example, within a partnership, at school, in a workplace, or online. A single incident can involve multiple forms in more than one setting.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Understanding what counts as GBV
text: Not every disagreement or financial difficulty is violence. To understand a concerning situation, consider whether there is coercion, intimidation, non-consent, a pattern of domination, threats or intentional harm, and the wider context. A survivor should not be expected to collect evidence or label their experience before they deserve respectful support.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Physical violence
text: Physical violence includes using physical force to injure, hurt, frighten, restrain, or control another person. It may include pushing, hitting, kicking, burning, restraining someone against their will, or preventing access to necessary medical care. Physical violence is serious even when it leaves no visible mark. [2,4]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Physical violence
text: Visible injuries are not required for someone to experience harm. Conversely, an injury alone does not establish who caused it; professional assessment should be sensitive to context and safety. Assault involving strangulation or pressure to the neck may cause serious injury even without obvious marks and needs urgent medical assessment.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Sexual violence and sexual coercion
text: Sexual violence involves sexual acts, attempted acts or unwanted sexual contact or attention imposed without free agreement, including by force, threats, manipulation, or misuse of authority. It may be committed by a stranger, acquaintance, spouse, partner, teacher, supervisor or other person. Being in a marriage or relationship does not create permanent consent. [1,3,7]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Sexual violence and sexual coercion
text: Consent must be freely given, informed, specific and revocable. Silence, fear, freezing, previous agreement, intoxication, or dependence on another person do not establish freely given consent. The legal treatment of specific acts and ages varies by jurisdiction; trained local practitioners must interpret relevant laws.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Sexual violence and sexual coercion
text: Sexual harassment can involve unwelcome sexual comments, pressure, messages, advances or touching. Sexual exploitation involves abusing a position of vulnerability, trust or authority for sexual purposes. Examples include demanding sexual favors in exchange for a job opportunity or essential assistance. Children need child-protection responses, and adults should never ask children to describe abuse in detail outside a trained safeguarding process.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Psychological and emotional violence
text: Psychological abuse involves actions that intimidate, degrade, manipulate, isolate, threaten or undermine a person. Emotional abuse is commonly used to describe repeated humiliation, belittling, threats, guilt-based control, or attacks on self-worth. These terms overlap; one incident or pattern may cause harm even without physical violence. [2,3,4]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Psychological and emotional violence
text: Examples include threats of harm, repeated insults, forcing isolation from family, using children to threaten a caregiver, or deliberately creating fear. “Gaslighting” is a non-clinical popular term often used for attempts to cause someone to doubt their perceptions; it should not replace clear descriptions of actual conduct. It is important not to diagnose an entire relationship from a single insensitive comment. Look instead at coercion, power, repeated behavior, the ability to disagree safely, and impact on autonomy. No one needs a formal label to ask for support.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Economic and financial abuse
text: Economic abuse uses money, access to work, education, property or essential resources to limit a person’s independence or control their decisions. It can include confiscating earnings, denying access to basic necessities as punishment, sabotaging employment, coercing debt, or preventing someone from attending school. [2,3]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Economic and financial abuse
text: Economic abuse is not identical to poverty or a jointly agreed household budget. The distinguishing concern is coercive restriction, exploitation or deprivation rather than limited income alone. A person may be unable to leave an unsafe relationship because of dependent children, lack of transport, housing insecurity or fear of losing school fees.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Technology-facilitated GBV
text: Technology-facilitated abuse uses phones, social media, messaging platforms, location-sharing services or other digital tools to threaten, track, shame, exploit or control a person. Offline and online forms often overlap. Some acts include repeated threatening messages, unauthorized access to accounts, tracking location without consent, publication of private information, and sharing intimate images without permission. [2,5]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Technology-facilitated GBV
text: A person experiencing technology-facilitated abuse may fear that changing passwords, deleting an app or blocking someone could escalate danger. Safety decisions should consider whether the other person has device access or controls accounts. Digital safety guidance should be personalized by a trained practitioner when risk is high.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Social, reproductive and identity-related coercion
text: Some violence occurs through controlling social participation, mobility, marriage choices or reproductive decisions. Examples include forced marriage, threats for refusing a relationship, interference with access to reproductive healthcare, or restricting movement for gender-based reasons. Forms of reproductive coercion may include pressure concerning pregnancy or contraception. [3,9]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Social, reproductive and identity-related coercion
text: People may also be targeted because they do not conform to gender expectations. Faith, family and cultural background can be important sources of resilience, but no cultural or religious justification excuses violence or forced participation. Local law, child protection rules and clinical practice must be checked before providing legal or medical instructions.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — How forms of GBV overlap
text: Forms of violence should not be treated as separate boxes. One individual may experience control of their finances, humiliation, threats of sexual harm and digital monitoring simultaneously. Understanding these connections helps avoid the mistaken belief that only physical injury makes an experience serious. The European Institute for Gender Equality describes a continuum of violence in which forms can reinforce one another. [6]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — How forms of GBV overlap
text: For example, a controlling partner may make a person financially dependent, demand constant location sharing, threaten family members and then use physical force when challenged. The overlapping pattern can create barriers to seeking help. No reader should be encouraged to test whether another person will become violent.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Recognizing risk without creating a checklist diagnosis
text: Warning signs include threats, escalating intimidation, forced isolation, monitoring, stalking, coercive sexual demands, unwanted physical restraint, and deliberate restriction of necessities. These signs help people notice possible danger but cannot predict an individual’s future actions reliably. Safety is a practical priority even when a situation does not fit a textbook pattern.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Recognizing risk without creating a checklist diagnosis
text: If someone is in immediate danger, the safest response may be to move toward a safer place and contact available emergency or specialist services, if doing so will not increase risk. Avoid telling a person to challenge an abuser, secretly record conversations or leave in a particular way; those decisions require context-sensitive planning.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Effects on survivors and why reactions differ
text: Possible consequences include injuries, fear, shame, distress, traumatic stress reactions, difficulty concentrating, disrupted education or work, reduced trust, financial loss and social isolation. Responses vary: some people disclose promptly, some remain silent, and others may show no obvious emotional reaction. None of these responses establishes whether harm occurred. [1,7]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Effects on survivors and why reactions differ
text: A person may remain in contact with someone who has harmed them because of threats, affection, children, finances, disability-related needs, lack of trusted services or other circumstances. Support should focus on informed choices and safety, not judging the survivor’s behavior.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Survivor-centred first-line support
text: WHO describes a structured approach known as LIVES: Listen, Inquire about needs and concerns, Validate, Enhance safety, and Support. This is a framework for trained providers; everyday supporters can adopt its respectful principles without undertaking an investigation or counselling role. [10]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Survivor-centred first-line support
text: Do not demand a detailed story, promise total secrecy, blame the survivor, press for forgiveness or reconciliation, or contact a suspected perpetrator without a safe and lawful basis. Professionals must explain confidentiality limits and child safeguarding or reporting obligations applicable to their work.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Helping children and adolescents safely
text: When a child may be experiencing violence, protection takes priority over adult learning activities. Do not interview repeatedly, ask leading questions, request images, or promise to keep everything secret. Listen calmly, explain what help may be needed in age-appropriate words, and contact a qualified child protection or health professional through established procedures. Children cannot be expected to manage adult safety plans independently.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Helping children and adolescents safely
text: In Rwanda, the Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion publishes the National Child Development Agency hotline 711. Availability and appropriate referral procedures should be verified at the time of use. [11]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Safe information seeking in Rwanda
text: Rwanda’s Isange One Stop Centres provide coordinated services that may include medical assistance, psychosocial support and justice-related services. UNHCR Rwanda lists a toll-free contact number of 3029 and notes that approaching a centre may result in a GBV incident being reported to law enforcement. A person should ask about confidentiality and reporting implications when it is safe to do so. [11,12]

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Safe information seeking in Rwanda
text: These contacts were checked against published pages on 9 November 2026. Telephone access, operating arrangements and referral rules can change. This handbook does not guarantee confidential treatment, availability or a particular legal outcome. A local specialist should verify them before public release.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Facilitator guidance and safeguarding
text: A facilitator should inform learners about potentially distressing content before a session. Participation in scenarios and reflections must be optional. Never ask for personal testimonies or facilitate public identification of survivors. Provide private, verified information about support channels; explain the limits of privacy and mandatory reporting. Train facilitators to respond calmly to unexpected disclosures and to refer rather than investigate.

title: Types and Forms of Gender-Based Violence — Key messages and glossary
text: Key messages. GBV has many interrelated forms. Visible injury is not required for harm to be serious. Consent and personal autonomy matter. A survivor deserves non-judgmental support whether or not they report an incident. Safe professional assistance can include health, protection, psychosocial and justice services, depending on needs and wishes.
