title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Understanding what drives GBV
text: GBV refers to harmful acts linked to gender-based expectations, discrimination, or unequal power relations. Research on violence against women and girls consistently identifies gender inequality as a structural driver, especially when beliefs about entitlement, control, and obedience make abuse seem acceptable or inevitable [1,2]. Other people, including men and boys, may experience gender-related abuse and deserve equally respectful support.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Understanding what drives GBV
text: It is useful to separate the conditions that allow violence from the decision to commit violence. A setting may tolerate intimidation or unequal authority; nevertheless, an individual who uses violence is responsible for that conduct. Poverty, alcohol use, jealousy, disagreement, or cultural tradition are never excuses.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Gender inequality and unequal power
text: Gender inequality describes unequal rights, opportunities, resources, expectations or influence associated with gender. It can operate through everyday decisions about who may study, work, own property, travel, speak in public, control money, or refuse sexual activity. The relationship to GBV becomes especially concerning when someone treats these inequalities as a right to dominate another person [1,3].

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Gender inequality and unequal power
text: Power itself is not violence. Parents, teachers, managers and public officials may hold legitimate responsibilities. Abuse occurs when a person misuses authority to threaten, exploit, isolate, humiliate, coerce, or harm someone. A manager who links a job opportunity to unwanted sexual conduct is misusing professional power. A partner who blocks access to shared finances to force obedience is using economic control.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Gender inequality and unequal power
text: Formal equality matters, but written rights do not by themselves eliminate harmful practices. Effective prevention also changes behavior, accountability, access to resources, and what people consider acceptable in everyday relationships.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Harmful norms and learned beliefs
text: Social norms are shared expectations about what people in a group typically do or approve of. Some norms protect dignity and collective care. Others create risk when they say that a partner must always obey, that jealousy proves love, that boys must be aggressive to be respected, or that reporting violence dishonors a family.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Harmful norms and learned beliefs
text: Children can learn these expectations through observation, jokes, peer pressure, media messages, social institutions, and how adults respond to conflict. However, seeing violence in childhood does not mean a person will inevitably become violent. It indicates a possible risk that supportive relationships, education and intervention can help address [2,4].

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — The ecological model: four connected levels
text: The social-ecological model used in public health examines how influences interact at the individual, relationship, community, and societal levels [2,4]. No single level explains every incident. Prevention becomes stronger when actions address several levels at once.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — The ecological model: four connected levels
text: Risk factors in a table are not labels to attach to individuals. A person experiencing unemployment or a mental health difficulty should never be assumed to be violent or likely to experience abuse. Assessment must be grounded in actual behavior and context.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Social and institutional influences
text: Where household roles give one person exclusive control over money, mobility, decisions, or communication, others may have fewer safe options. Unequal expectations about unpaid caregiving and earning income can reinforce dependency. Equal decision-making and accessible independent resources can reduce vulnerability without implying that every unequal household has violence.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Social and institutional influences
text: Rigid expectations about girls and boys, harassment dismissed as normal, and unequal power between learners and staff can contribute to risk. Prevention includes clear safeguarding codes, accessible confidential reporting, staff training, age-appropriate consent education, and protection against retaliation. Schools must not force survivors into public disclosures or face-to-face mediation with alleged perpetrators.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Social and institutional influences
text: Risks can emerge where supervisors can demand personal favors, threaten job loss, or manipulate pay and promotion. Effective measures include clear harassment policies, independent reporting channels, protection against retaliation, impartial investigation, and access to support. General awareness training without accountable procedures is insufficient.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Social and institutional influences
text: Community leaders, health workers, police, justice actors and faith leaders can support prevention when they refuse victim-blaming, protect confidentiality within its legal limits, and refer people appropriately. They can also cause harm if they pressure a survivor to reconcile, insist on a disclosure, or expose private information.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Economic pressures: association is not justification
text: Poverty, job insecurity, unequal control of assets, and inadequate access to housing or transport may intensify vulnerability or make it harder to leave an unsafe relationship. The evidence associates economic stress with some violence risks, but poverty does not automatically produce violence, nor are people experiencing economic hardship inherently abusive [1,5].

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Economic pressures: association is not justification
text: Financial empowerment can increase choice, but an intervention that changes household power dynamics may sometimes produce backlash. Programs should combine economic opportunities with gender-transformative approaches, consent, safety assessment, and routes to specialized support rather than assume that giving someone money alone guarantees safety.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Alcohol, substances, and violence
text: Harmful alcohol use is associated with some forms of violence and may intensify risk in particular circumstances [1,5]. However, many people who drink do not become violent, and many perpetrators use violence without consuming alcohol. The decision to threaten or assault someone remains the perpetrator’s responsibility. Prevention may include access to treatment for harmful substance use and measures that reduce hazardous drinking, but substance treatment should not replace accountability or protection for a person experiencing abuse.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Risk factors versus warning signs
text: A risk factor is a population-level association. A warning sign is a specific behavior or circumstance that may indicate abuse in a particular setting. Confusing the two can lead to discrimination or false reassurance.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Risk factors versus warning signs
text: Warning signs should lead to safe options and appropriate support, not public accusations or confrontations organized by untrained people. If someone is in immediate danger, urgent local assistance takes priority over educational discussion.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Protective factors and resilience
text: Protective conditions include relationships based on mutual respect; norms that reject violence; access to education and economic opportunities; trustworthy health, legal and psychosocial support; and rules that are fairly enforced [2,5]. No protective factor can guarantee that violence will never occur.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Protective factors and resilience
text: Supportive families and communities can reduce isolation, but survivors should retain control over whom they involve whenever possible. A person should not be required to disclose to a relative, partner, religious leader or community meeting before seeking specialist help.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Prevention based on evidence: the RESPECT framework
text: WHO and partners’ updated 2025 RESPECT framework identifies seven complementary approaches to preventing violence against women [2]. It is a population-level prevention framework, not a checklist for making an unsafe relationship safe.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Prevention based on evidence: the RESPECT framework
text: Programs should evaluate outcomes, not just count training sessions. Useful measures may include changes in acceptance of violence, safety of reporting, quality of referrals, implementation of protections, and carefully collected reports of harm. Collecting survivor disclosures for monitoring must never compromise confidentiality.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Rwanda relevance: local systems and approaches
text: Rwanda’s National Policy against Gender-Based Violence identifies prevention, survivor response, coordination and accountability as core areas [6]. A newer national strategy engaging men and boys emphasizes transforming harmful gender norms and promoting equitable responsibilities [3]. These documents provide useful local grounding, but a program must confirm current legal duties, operational procedures and official referral contacts with responsible national institutions.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Rwanda relevance: local systems and approaches
text: For VUGA NDAKUMVA, examples should reflect the diversity of Rwandan settings: urban and rural households, schools, informal work, agriculture, workplaces, and digital communication. Avoid presenting any district, cultural practice, occupation, age group, or income bracket as inherently violent.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Rwanda relevance: local systems and approaches
text: When someone asks for GBV help, direct them to verified local specialist support, including Isange One Stop Centres where available, while taking their immediate safety and privacy into account. Do not publish unverified hotlines or promise that all providers offer identical services at all hours.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Supporting a person safely
text: A person asking about GBV may be seeking general knowledge or may be living with current danger. An educator should avoid guessing. Offer a choice to continue learning or discuss safe help-seeking, do not ask for unnecessary details, and explain confidentiality and its limits. A survivor should never be blamed for a decision to stay, leave, report, or delay action.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Safe communication and sensitive data
text: Education and outreach must consider that a controlling person may access another person’s phone or browsing history. Public materials should not assume that a user can safely keep an app open, receive notifications, or save phone numbers. Digital safety measures may help, but no quick-exit feature can guarantee that browsing history or monitoring has been erased.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Safe communication and sensitive data
text: For workshops and surveys, do not collect real-life disclosures as a learning requirement. If someone voluntarily discloses violence, follow an approved safeguarding protocol. For minors, follow locally applicable child-protection and reporting obligations, explained in an age-appropriate way.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Short glossary
text: Gender inequality: Unequal access to opportunities, resources, rights or influence on the basis of gender.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Short glossary
text: Gender norm: A socially shared expectation about how people of different genders should behave.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Short glossary
text: Coercive control: A pattern of threatening, isolating or restricting behavior aimed at dominating someone.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Short glossary
text: Risk factor: A condition associated with increased likelihood of an outcome in research.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Short glossary
text: Protective factor: A condition associated with reduced risk or increased safety.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Short glossary
text: Ecological model: A framework that considers individual, relationship, community and societal influences.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Short glossary
text: Survivor-centred: An approach prioritizing the person’s dignity, safety, rights, privacy and informed choices.

title: Root Causes, Risk Factors, and Gender Inequality — Short glossary
text: Prevention: Actions designed to reduce the occurrence of violence and the conditions that enable it.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — What consent means
text: Consent is a person’s voluntary, informed agreement to a specific action or interaction. The person must be able to understand the choice and make it without threats, manipulation or other coercion. Agreement should be communicated clearly, checked when uncertain, and revisited when circumstances change. Consent is a process of respectful communication, not a signature, ownership right, or permanent permission. [1, 2]

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — What consent means
text: Consent matters in everyday life—touch, photographs, sharing personal information, medical decisions and financial interactions. Sexual consent has special ethical and legal importance. The fact that someone accepts one activity does not give permission for another.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — What consent means
text: These principles are useful educational guidelines; legal tests and definitions depend on the applicable law and the circumstances. [1, 2, 3]

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Consent, choice and capacity
text: A meaningful choice requires more than a spoken “yes.” The setting must permit a real refusal. A person who is asleep, unconscious or otherwise unable to understand or decide cannot provide consent. Severe intoxication or incapacity can undermine the ability to consent; the precise legal threshold requires case-specific assessment under applicable law. [1, 2]

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Consent, choice and capacity
text: Children have additional legal and safeguarding protections. Adult concepts of sexual agreement must never be used to imply that a child can legally consent to sexual activity with an adult. Age-of-consent and reporting obligations must be checked against current Rwanda law by a qualified local reviewer before publication.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Consent, choice and capacity
text: Someone may become quiet, freeze, comply out of fear, or appear calm while feeling unsafe. None of these responses proves agreement. A supportive person must not infer consent from a lack of resistance; when uncertainty exists, pause and check, and stop if there is no clear freely given agreement. A survivor should never be blamed for freezing or not physically resisting.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Personal boundaries: understanding and expressing limits
text: A boundary is a limit that helps a person decide what they are comfortable sharing, doing, giving or receiving. Boundaries may differ across people and situations; they can change over time. A respectful boundary names what is acceptable and, when useful, what action the person will take to protect their wellbeing. Respect for others is equally important.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Personal boundaries: understanding and expressing limits
text: “I do not want to be hugged today.” “Please ask before posting my photo.” “I am not comfortable sharing my password.” “I need to end this conversation for now.” “I can help tomorrow, but I cannot do it tonight.” People experiencing violence may be unable to express boundaries safely. It is not their responsibility to confront someone who may retaliate. Safety takes priority over boundary-setting exercises.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Bodily autonomy and dignity
text: Bodily autonomy is the principle that people should be able to make decisions about their own bodies free from violence and coercion, within applicable laws and protections. It includes the right to personal safety, respect during healthcare, and freedom from unwanted contact. For children and people needing decision-making support, autonomy must be understood alongside safeguarding, accessible communication, and relevant legal requirements.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Bodily autonomy and dignity
text: Respecting bodily autonomy means asking before touching where appropriate, explaining proposed medical or intimate actions, and responding when a person expresses discomfort. A person’s clothing, relationship status, disability, prior sexual experience, or dependence on others does not cancel the need for consent.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Coercion, manipulation and power imbalances
text: Coercion occurs when a person uses force, threats, intimidation, persistent pressure or exploitation of vulnerability to influence another person’s choice. It may be physical, emotional, economic, social or digital. A statement that sounds like agreement may not represent voluntary consent if the alternative involves harm, punishment, lost housing or other serious consequences.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Coercion, manipulation and power imbalances
text: Power differences do not automatically make every relationship abusive, but they can make it harder to refuse or raise concerns. Institutions should provide reporting channels that do not require confronting the person with authority.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Consent in dating, marriage and long-term relationships
text: Marriage, engagement, dating, cohabitation or previous sexual contact never creates permanent consent. Each person retains the right to refuse sexual activity. A respectful partner asks rather than assumes, accepts “no,” and does not punish refusal through anger, humiliation or financial threats. [3, 4] A relationship disagreement is not automatically GBV. However, repeated threats, forced sexual contact, intimidation and control are significant warning signs. Supporters should examine safety and patterns of control rather than telling a survivor to “communicate better” with an abusive partner.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Consent in dating, marriage and long-term relationships
text: Questions such as “Are you comfortable with this?”, “Do you want to continue?”, and “Would you prefer to stop?” create space for choice. If a person hesitates or appears afraid, stop and avoid pressure. Agreement to intimacy is not consent to contraception interference, recordings, or dissemination of private material.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Digital consent, privacy and technology
text: Digital consent applies when sharing photographs, recordings, messages, account access, contact information, and location data. Permission to create a photo is not permission to publish or forward it. Permission to use a shared device is not permission to read private messages or track movements. Technology-facilitated GBV may include harassment, stalking, impersonation, threats, and non-consensual sharing of intimate images. [5]

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Digital consent, privacy and technology
text: Practical safety options depend on context. For someone whose devices may be monitored, changing a password, deleting messages or confronting a suspected abuser could increase danger. Consider using a trusted device and obtaining confidential support. Do not assume a “quick exit” button erases browsing history or makes a device safe.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Culture, social expectations and unequal power
text: Families and communities differ in how they discuss personal space, sexuality and authority. Cultural values such as mutual care and respect can strengthen prevention, while expectations demanding unquestioning obedience or tolerating abuse can undermine choice. Education should avoid stereotyping any community and should encourage discussion without forcing personal disclosures.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Culture, social expectations and unequal power
text: In Rwanda, examples may involve university accommodation, workplace apprenticeships, household decision-making, transportation, or online relationships. The examples below are fictional and do not represent prevalence claims about any specific group.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — How to respond when someone describes coercion
text: Listen with care and without interrogation. Ask what the person needs right now. Affirm that they deserve safety and respect without making promises about outcomes. Explain confidentiality limits, ask permission before making referrals wherever possible, and consider whether the person can safely receive calls or messages. WHO’s LIVES approach offers a clinical first-line support structure: Listen, Inquire about needs and concerns, Validate, Enhance safety, and Support. [4, 6]

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Safety considerations and seeking support
text: If someone is in immediate danger or has a serious injury, urgent local emergency or medical assistance is appropriate. After sexual assault, prompt medical attention can address injury and time-sensitive preventive care; survivors can request information about medical options even when unsure about reporting. Do not delay urgent care to complete exercises, preserve evidence or finish reading this chapter.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Safety considerations and seeking support
text: In Rwanda, Isange One Stop Centres are an important integrated service model for survivors of GBV. Local organizations should verify current access details, telephone numbers, hours, referral criteria, and statutory reporting duties before publishing public instructions. This chapter deliberately avoids unverified hotlines and jurisdiction-specific reporting promises.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Safety considerations and seeking support
text: For children, suspected abuse, or a person unable to make certain decisions, safeguarding duties may differ from those for adults. Do not promise absolute secrecy. Explain relevant protections and reporting requirements in age-appropriate language, and involve qualified safeguarding professionals.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Facilitator notes and accessibility
text: Use plain language, short sessions, and inclusive examples. Allow written, spoken or private participation. Provide alternatives to pair work, and do not ask anyone to demonstrate consent through physical touch. An educator should never invite public disclosures of abuse. Establish a quiet opt-out option and identify an appropriate safeguarding contact before group sessions.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Facilitator notes and accessibility
text: Translate carefully into Kinyarwanda and French. Concepts such as coercion, autonomy, consent and abuse may not map perfectly word-for-word. Have a qualified local language reviewer and GBV professional review both terminology and examples. For screen readers, keep headings logical and avoid image-only explanations.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Key terms
text: Consent: Voluntary, informed agreement to a specific act, communicated by someone able to decide.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Key terms
text: Bodily autonomy: The principle that a person should have agency over decisions involving their body, subject to appropriate legal protections.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Key terms
text: Boundary: A limit describing what a person is comfortable with or willing to do.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Key terms
text: Coercion: Force, threats, pressure or exploitation that undermines meaningful free choice.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Key terms
text: Power imbalance: A relationship where one person has substantially greater control over resources, status or decisions.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Key terms
text: Digital consent: Agreement about access, use or sharing of digital information, images and communications.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Key terms
text: Survivor-centred care: An approach prioritizing dignity, safety, confidentiality within its limits, respect and informed choice.

title: Understanding Consent, Boundaries, and Bodily Autonomy — Publication approval checklist
text: Editorial caution: This document teaches principles and examples. It does not determine whether a particular incident constitutes an offence, and it is not a substitute for emergency support, clinical care or qualified legal advice.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Understanding domestic violence
text: Domestic violence describes abusive behavior occurring within domestic or family relationships. Depending on legal definitions and setting, it may involve spouses, partners, former partners, parents, adult children, siblings, or other household or family members. It can include physical harm and patterns of threats, intimidation, sexual coercion, controlling behavior, or economic restrictions.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Understanding domestic violence
text: Intimate partner violence (IPV) refers to behavior by a current or former intimate partner that causes physical, sexual, or psychological harm, including acts of aggression, sexual coercion, psychological abuse and controlling behaviors. IPV can occur within marriage or dating relationships, including after separation. It is not limited to couples who live together. [1,2]

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Understanding domestic violence
text: Many domestic violence incidents are gender-based, especially where violence enforces unequal gender power or expectations; however, the terms domestic violence and GBV are not identical. Anyone affected by abuse deserves support. Population-level evidence shows that women and girls are disproportionately affected by intimate partner and sexual violence. [1]

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Understanding domestic violence
text: Two people may disagree, become frustrated, or need time apart without committing abuse. Abuse involves conduct that harms, threatens, coerces, intimidates, or restricts another person’s autonomy. A repeated pattern of surveillance, humiliation, isolation, or punishment for saying “no” is concerning even when there are no visible injuries. An isolated incident of severe violence is also serious; it need not recur to warrant help.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Understanding domestic violence
text: Remember: Violence is a choice made by the person using abusive behavior. Stress, alcohol, jealousy, poverty, family difficulties, or a survivor’s decision do not justify abuse.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Forms of violence within relationships
text: Physical violence includes hitting, slapping, kicking, choking or strangulation, pushing, restraining, using a weapon, throwing objects to injure, or preventing a person from escaping. Serious harm may occur without visible marks. A person subjected to pressure on the neck requires urgent medical evaluation because dangerous complications can occur even when symptoms initially seem minor.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Forms of violence within relationships
text: Sexual violence includes any sexual act or contact without freely given agreement, including within marriage or a long-term relationship. Threats, force, fear, intoxication, exploitation of authority, and other forms of coercion can undermine consent. Reproductive coercion may involve sabotaging contraception, pressuring someone about pregnancy outcomes, or restricting reproductive healthcare choices.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Forms of violence within relationships
text: This may involve repeated threats, humiliation, insults, intimidation, blaming a person for the abusive behavior, threatening to harm children or loved ones, or making the person doubt their perceptions. Persistent isolation from friends, family, education, or work can also function as control. The purpose or effect may be to create fear and dependence.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Forms of violence within relationships
text: Economic abuse may include preventing someone from earning income, taking wages, hiding essential documents, controlling access to food or transport, or creating debt in the other person’s name. Digital abuse may include monitoring messages, demanding passwords, tracking location, impersonation, harassment, or threatening to publish private images. Technology can make controlling behavior continue after physical separation.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — What is coercive control?
text: Coercive control is an ongoing pattern of intimidation, isolation, monitoring, restrictions, or punishment that progressively reduces a person’s freedom and ability to make choices. A person may appear to “agree” with demands because refusal could trigger threats or harm. The pattern often matters more than any single action.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — What is coercive control?
text: Not every request, shared financial decision, or relationship disagreement is abuse. Consider context, freedom to decline, retaliation, repeated patterns, and whether one person is afraid of the consequences of saying no.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Recognizing warning signs and escalation
text: Warning signs include increasing monitoring, repeated threats, humiliating comments, forced sex, physical assaults, threats with weapons, stalking, isolation, and interference with work or medical care. A person may minimize danger because the behavior has developed gradually, or because periods of kindness alternate with abuse.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Recognizing warning signs and escalation
text: Particularly concerning signals include threats to kill, strangulation, access to weapons, forced sex, escalating frequency or severity of violence, stalking after separation, or a survivor expressing fear of imminent serious harm. These signals call for urgent professional safety assessment where possible. Neither an online checklist nor a community volunteer should attempt to predict danger with certainty.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Recognizing warning signs and escalation
text: Immediate priority: If there is immediate danger, prioritize reaching a safer place and contacting emergency assistance when it is safe to do so. Do not confront the suspected abusive person or advise a supporter to intervene physically.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Effects on health, dignity, and daily life
text: Domestic and intimate partner violence can cause injury, chronic pain, reproductive-health problems, anxiety, depression, traumatic stress, sleep disruption, reduced school or work participation, and financial insecurity. Not every survivor experiences all these outcomes. Survivors may also show resilience, maintain responsibilities, or appear calm while facing significant risk. [1]

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Effects on health, dignity, and daily life
text: Children exposed to violence in the household may experience fear, sleep or concentration difficulties, school disruption, and emotional or behavioral problems. Their needs must be assessed independently, with appropriate child protection procedures. Exposure does not predetermine their future behavior or wellbeing.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Effects on health, dignity, and daily life
text: Reasons can include threats of retaliation, concern for children, financial dependence, housing insecurity, social pressure, disability-related barriers, lack of confidential services, immigration or documentation concerns, and emotional attachment. Leaving a controlling relationship can sometimes increase short-term danger. A survivor should never be blamed for staying, returning, or asking for help more than once.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Risk factors are not excuses
text: Research identifies influences at individual, relationship, community, and societal levels. Inequitable gender norms, acceptance of violence, prior exposure to abuse, harmful alcohol use, and weak institutional accountability can be associated with greater risk. No single factor explains an individual abusive act; many people facing the same difficulties never use violence. [1,4]

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Risk factors are not excuses
text: Prevention requires action beyond individuals: respectful relationship education, accessible services, safe environments, economic opportunity, accountable institutions, and gender-equitable norms. WHO’s RESPECT framework presents seven complementary prevention strategies. [4]

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Safe, survivor-centred first-line support
text: WHO first-line support emphasizes meeting immediate emotional and physical needs, ongoing safety, and continuing support. The LIVES framework is useful for trained helpers and can also inform respectful responses by trusted supporters. [2,3]

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Safe, survivor-centred first-line support
text: Supporters should not investigate the incident, promise outcomes, attempt couples mediation where coercion or violence is present, or contact an abusive partner without the survivor’s informed and safe participation. Child protection and mandatory reporting requirements may affect confidentiality; professionals must explain applicable limits.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Safety planning: principles, not a fixed script
text: Safety planning should be individualized, ideally with a trained GBV service provider, because apparently ordinary advice can increase risk. A plan may consider where the person can go in an emergency, trusted contacts, safe transport, medical needs, children’s needs, documents, money, and whether communication devices are monitored. The survivor chooses what is appropriate for their circumstances.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Safety planning: principles, not a fixed script
text: Do not advise a person to save a visible list of “escape steps” on a monitored phone, secretly record someone in ways that may be unsafe or unlawful, or confront the abusive person to announce a plan. Clearing browsing history does not always remove traces of activity. Where appropriate, a safer phone or a trusted professional service may reduce exposure.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Safety planning: principles, not a fixed script
text: A former partner may continue harassment, tracking, threats, or economic coercion. Support should consider digital privacy, safe communication, childcare and school arrangements, and legal assistance. Decisions about protection measures should be discussed with qualified local providers, not determined by a generic online guide.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Health care and urgent situations
text: Medical assessment is important after injuries, strangulation, sexual assault, severe distress, or new concerning symptoms. After sexual violence, timely professional care can address injuries, sexually transmitted infection prevention, emergency contraception where appropriate and available, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis when clinically indicated, and forensic options. Some interventions are time-sensitive; do not wait for legal decisions before seeking medical advice. [2,3]

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Health care and urgent situations
text: The patient should be treated with dignity and informed of what examinations, documentation, and reporting procedures may involve. Whether reporting is voluntary or required depends on applicable law and safeguarding responsibilities; providers should explain the situation clearly.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Health care and urgent situations
text: Do not use this handbook to make clinical decisions. Symptoms such as difficulty breathing, severe bleeding, loss of consciousness, head injury, or concerning signs after neck compression need emergency assessment. A qualified health professional must evaluate treatment needs.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Accessing help in Rwanda
text: Rwanda’s Isange One Stop Centre model brings together medical, psychosocial, investigative, and legal services for GBV survivors and people affected by child abuse. MIGEPROF describes centres nationwide, while the Rwanda Investigation Bureau publishes current contact lines. UNHCR cautions that visiting an Isange centre may involve reporting to law enforcement; survivors should ask about confidentiality and reporting processes. [5,6,7]

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Accessing help in Rwanda
text: These numbers are published by the indicated authorities as of the chapter’s November 2026 source review. Availability, operating procedures and eligibility should be checked before relying on them. VUGA NDAKUMVA should maintain a verified referral directory and never imply a guaranteed response time. [5,6]

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Editorial and professional review before publication
text: This document is a complete reader-facing educational material, not an approved intervention protocol. Before public release, obtain review from a qualified GBV/safeguarding professional, a clinician for health content, and an appropriate Rwanda legal or referral specialist. Verify local service operating hours, confidentiality and reporting procedures, terminology, accessibility, and Kinyarwanda and French adaptations. Keep a record of the reviewer, approval date, changes and next review date.

title: Domestic Violence and Intimate Partner Violence — Editorial and professional review before publication
text: Next chapter: GBV Chapter 06 - Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation. Develop it separately after Chapter 05 editorial review, with special medical, child safeguarding, and legal input.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Understanding sexual violence
text: Sexual violence refers to sexual acts, attempted sexual acts, or other sexual conduct carried out without valid consent, including through force, threats, intimidation, coercion, exploitation of vulnerability, or abuse of power. It can happen between strangers, acquaintances, relatives, colleagues, partners, or spouses. It may occur in person or through technology. Sexual violence is never justified by a person’s clothing, relationship history, social status, or previous consent. [1, 2]

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Understanding sexual violence
text: Sexual violence is not limited to physically violent assault. It may involve unwanted sexual touching, forced or coerced sexual activity, attempted sexual assault, sexual exploitation, or non-consensual creation or sharing of sexual images. The exact legal definitions and offences differ by jurisdiction and must be checked against Rwandan law when legal information is published.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Consent: what makes agreement meaningful?
text: Consent is a freely given, informed, specific and ongoing agreement to a particular activity. Someone may change their mind. Being married, dating, accepting a gift, going to someone’s room, or agreeing to one activity does not imply agreement to another. Silence, freezing, or absence of physical resistance is not by itself consent. [1, 2]

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Consent: what makes agreement meaningful?
text: The age and capacity of a child require separate safeguarding and legal rules. A child’s apparent agreement does not remove the need for child protection and legal assessment.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Sexual harassment
text: Sexual harassment includes unwelcome sexual comments, requests, messages, gestures, images, touching, or other sexual conduct that violates dignity or creates an intimidating, hostile, humiliating, or offensive environment. It can occur in schools, workplaces, public transport, markets, health facilities, community organizations, or online spaces.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Sexual harassment
text: Pressure linked to rewards or penalties: A person with authority requests sexual contact in exchange for a grade, placement, promotion, contract, or service. Hostile environment: Repeated sexual jokes, unwanted advances or degrading conduct make studying or working unsafe. A single serious incident can also warrant attention.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Sexual harassment
text: Examples: A lecturer repeatedly sends sexual messages to a student after being asked to stop; a manager threatens to reduce shifts following a rejected advance; commuters make unwanted sexual contact on a bus. The person experiencing harassment is not responsible for managing the offender’s behavior.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Sexual exploitation and abuse of authority
text: Sexual exploitation involves abusing a position of vulnerability, differential power, or trust for sexual purposes, including situations in which a person seeks sexual access or advantage by controlling something the other person needs. A person may appear to agree while facing severe inequality in available choices. [3] An aid worker who conditions assistance on sexual acts, a recruiter who demands sexual favors for employment, or a caretaker who uses dependence to pressure someone are illustrative forms of exploitation. Such conduct may also breach safeguarding obligations, professional ethics, and criminal law.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Sexual exploitation and abuse of authority
text: Power can come from grades, money, employment, legal or immigration status, access to food and shelter, professional authority, social influence, physical strength, or control over confidential information. Ethical organizations must define prohibitions, reporting routes, retaliation protections, and independent responses instead of leaving an affected person to negotiate with the person holding power.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Sexual coercion and intimidation
text: Coercion is pressure that undermines a person’s freedom to choose. It can include threats of violence, blackmail, threats to disclose intimate images, persistent pressure after refusal, threats to withdraw financial support, manipulation of dependency, or abuse of institutional authority. Coercion can occur without visible injury.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Sexual coercion and intimidation
text: A healthy boundary is respected without argument, retaliation, or punishment. Repeated requests after a refusal, monitoring a person’s movements, or threatening their reputation should be treated as concerning behavior rather than romantic persistence.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Technology-facilitated sexual harm
text: Sexual harassment and coercion may occur through messaging, social networks, devices, and digital services. Examples include unsolicited sexual messages, demands for intimate photos, threats to publish images, sharing private sexual images without consent, impersonation, location-based stalking, or harassment across multiple accounts.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Technology-facilitated sexual harm
text: A person can consent to taking a photograph without consenting to its publication. Consent to share one message or image does not authorize redistribution. People experiencing digital abuse may need a tailored safety plan, especially if an offender can access their device or accounts.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Effects on wellbeing and daily life
text: Responses to sexual violence differ. Some survivors feel fear, anger, shame, sadness, numbness, or confusion; others may initially show little visible distress. Possible effects include injury, sexually transmitted infections, unintended pregnancy, sleep problems, traumatic stress, difficulty concentrating, withdrawal, and disruptions to education, work, and relationships. These are possible outcomes, not inevitable outcomes or criteria for believing someone.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Effects on wellbeing and daily life
text: People may delay disclosing because of fear, dependence, stigma, threats, family pressure, lack of safe services, or uncertainty about confidentiality. A delayed disclosure or fragmented memory does not prove an account false. Support should not depend on whether someone reports to police.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Responding to a disclosure: first-line support
text: The WHO clinical handbook emphasizes attention to immediate emotional needs, physical needs, ongoing safety, and longer-term support. The LIVES approach summarizes listening, inquiring about needs and concerns, validating, enhancing safety, and supporting access to services. These are principles for trained responders and should not be confused with conducting an investigation. [1]

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Responding to a disclosure: first-line support
text: Do not ask why the survivor was in a location, why they did not fight, or why they waited to disclose. Do not request a repeated account merely to satisfy curiosity, offer guarantees about outcomes, or promise absolute secrecy. Do not mediate between survivor and alleged offender as a substitute for protection and professional response.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Urgent healthcare after sexual assault
text: Time matters: If sexual assault was recent, seek medical care as soon as safely possible, ideally immediately. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), when clinically indicated, should start as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after a potential exposure. Emergency contraception may also be time-sensitive; a clinician should advise on available methods and their effective windows. Even after these windows, medical care and support remain important. [4, 5] Healthcare assessment may include treatment of injuries, assessment for HIV PEP, prevention or testing for sexually transmitted infections, emergency contraception where appropriate, other reproductive healthcare, psychological first-line support, and discussion of forensic documentation. The survivor should receive information and be asked for consent to examinations and procedures, subject to applicable safeguarding and legal requirements. [1, 4]

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Urgent healthcare after sexual assault
text: Do not delay medical care because you are unsure whether to report to police, or because clothing was changed or washing has occurred. Evidence options can be discussed by trained local providers. If someone is bleeding heavily, has severe injuries, is unconscious, or faces imminent danger, emergency care is the priority.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Safeguarding children and other vulnerable people
text: Children require an age-appropriate, trained response that prioritizes protection, avoids suggestive questioning, and follows applicable mandatory reporting, consent, and guardian rules. An accompanying adult is not always a safe guardian. Avoid asking the child to repeat a detailed account; record only essential facts according to authorized procedures and refer promptly to designated protection professionals.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Safeguarding children and other vulnerable people
text: People with disabilities, displaced persons, people dependent on caregivers, and others facing barriers may need accessible communication, interpreters, safe transport, or independent advocacy. Never assume that a survivor cannot make decisions merely because they need support.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Rwanda: care and referral pathways
text: Rwanda’s Isange One Stop Centres provide integrated services for GBV survivors, bringing together healthcare, psychosocial support, investigation and legal pathways. Government sources describe services as free and available through the national network. [6, 7]

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Rwanda: care and referral pathways
text: Important: UNHCR Rwanda notes that approaching an Isange Centre may lead to a report to law enforcement. Service users should ask how information will be shared and what confidentiality or child-protection obligations apply. Do not promise that a particular referral is anonymous or will avoid police involvement. [6, 7, 8]

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Prevention in schools, workplaces, and institutions
text: Preventing sexual harassment and exploitation requires clear rules and accountable systems, not only individual awareness. Educational institutions and employers should prohibit sexual demands linked to grades, placement, aid, recruitment, or promotion; train staff; provide confidential and accessible reporting channels; protect complainants and witnesses from retaliation; and arrange independent, timely, fair responses. A safe learning environment includes respectful boundaries, transparent assessment procedures, safeguarding responsibilities, and accessible support for students. A workplace should establish clear behavioral expectations and make reporting possible without forcing disclosure to the alleged offender’s supervisor.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Key terms
text: Consent: Freely given, informed and specific agreement that can be withdrawn.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Key terms
text: Sexual coercion: Pressure, threats or exploitation that undermines a free choice.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Key terms
text: Sexual harassment: Unwelcome sexual conduct that violates dignity or creates an intimidating or offensive environment.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Key terms
text: Sexual exploitation: Abuse of vulnerability, power or trust for sexual purposes.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Key terms
text: Safeguarding: Policies and actions intended to prevent and respond to harm, especially involving children and vulnerable people.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Key terms
text: PEP: Time-sensitive antiretroviral medication used after a possible HIV exposure when clinically indicated.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Key terms
text: Survivor-centred support: Support grounded in dignity, safety, privacy, informed choice and appropriate services.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Key terms
text: Forensic documentation: Professional medical and evidentiary records collected under applicable procedures and consent requirements.

title: Sexual Violence, Harassment, and Exploitation — Publication and specialist review checklist
text: End of Chapter 06. This educational material does not replace clinical care, survivor advocacy, emergency services or legal advice.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Understanding non-physical abuse
text: Emotional and psychological abuse refers to behavior intended to frighten, degrade, manipulate, isolate, or control someone, or behavior that has these effects within a pattern of coercion. Verbal abuse can include repeated insults, threats, humiliation, or degrading language. The terms overlap: verbal abuse describes one way harm may be expressed, while psychological abuse can also involve nonverbal threats, isolation, surveillance, and restrictions on freedom. [1, 2, 3]

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Understanding non-physical abuse
text: Abuse is not defined solely by whether a person shouts. A calm threat, deliberate humiliation in public, or repeated manipulation can be frightening and controlling. Conversely, a single argument, disappointment or respectfully expressed criticism does not automatically establish an abusive pattern. Context, impact, power, intent, repetition, fear and control all matter. One serious threat can also be dangerous even without a long history.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Understanding non-physical abuse
text: Abuse can be gender-based when it is linked to gender, gender expectations, discrimination or unequal gender-related power. People of any gender can be harmed. The fact that someone experiences harsh words does not on its own establish GBV; the surrounding context is essential. [1]

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Verbal abuse versus respectful conflict
text: Conflict happens in many relationships. People can disagree, express anger and set firm boundaries without using abuse. Healthy disagreements leave room for each person to speak, say no, seek support and make independent choices. Abuse may involve fear, repeated degradation, punishment for disagreement or behavior designed to control another person.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Verbal abuse versus respectful conflict
text: The goal is not to label every difficult interaction. It is to notice patterns of fear, coercion and reduced freedom, and to seek appropriate assessment or support when needed.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Coercive control: understanding the pattern
text: Coercive control is a pattern of behavior that restricts another person’s autonomy through fear, threats, monitoring, isolation or dependency. Several seemingly small acts may accumulate into a serious loss of freedom. A person may begin avoiding ordinary activities simply to prevent retaliation. [2, 3]

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Coercive control: understanding the pattern
text: For example, a partner may gradually demand passwords, decide who may visit, discourage employment and threaten humiliation if challenged. None of these acts needs to involve a physical injury to create risk. Coercive control can occur alongside physical or sexual violence, and escalation may be unpredictable.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Manipulation and reality-distorting behavior
text: Manipulation uses pressure, guilt, fear, misleading information or emotional leverage to influence decisions. Some abusive behavior involves consistently denying events, changing explanations, or making someone question their memory and judgment. The popular term “gaslighting” is sometimes used for such patterns, but it should not replace a careful description of actual actions.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Manipulation and reality-distorting behavior
text: A safe response focuses on observable behavior and its effects. Do not insist that someone confront an abusive person, gather evidence on a monitored device, or win an argument about what “really happened”.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Threats, humiliation and intimidation
text: Threats may be direct (“I will hurt you”) or indirect (“You will see what happens if you tell anyone”). A threat to remove children, end access to money, disclose private information or damage someone’s reputation can be used to exert control. Humiliation and name-calling may erode confidence and lead to withdrawal, while intimidation may make a person feel unsafe even without physical contact. [2]

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Threats, humiliation and intimidation
text: Threats involving weapons, serious violence, stalking, confinement, or harm to children require urgent attention. A survivor’s own assessment of danger deserves serious consideration. No public handbook can accurately predict an individual’s risk.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Emotional abuse in different settings
text: Repeated insults, isolation, monitoring, threats, blaming and restrictions on freedom can occur in marriages, dating relationships and other family contexts. Family reputation, financial interdependence or child-care responsibilities may complicate choices. The person harmed should not be blamed for staying, leaving, returning, or delaying disclosure.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Emotional abuse in different settings
text: An adult or peer may use humiliation, threats, rumor-spreading or promises of academic advantage to control a learner. An unequal position of authority can make refusal difficult. Education providers need safe reporting channels that protect learners from retaliation, particularly where minors are involved.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Emotional abuse in different settings
text: Abusive behavior may include repeated public degradation, threats to employment, discriminatory insults, isolation from colleagues or retaliation for raising concerns. Not every unfair workplace decision is necessarily GBV; assess the behavior and gender-related context. Workers may need independent reporting and support options.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Emotional abuse in different settings
text: Emotional abuse can continue through excessive messaging, threats, impersonation, public humiliation, monitoring or coercive access to accounts. Digital risks may increase if a person tries to change settings on a device the other person controls.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Possible effects on survivors
text: Non-physical abuse can be associated with fear, anxiety, low confidence, sleep disruption, social isolation, difficulties concentrating and reduced participation at school or work. Some people experience depression or trauma-related symptoms, but no specific reaction proves that abuse occurred. Responses differ, and a person may function outwardly while experiencing serious harm. [1, 2]

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Possible effects on survivors
text: Psychological symptoms are not a diagnosis. A qualified clinician should evaluate persistent or serious mental health symptoms, and medical or psychosocial assistance should be offered according to the person’s needs and wishes.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Why leaving or reporting may be difficult
text: People experiencing abuse may face threats, economic dependence, concerns for children, social stigma, disability-related barriers, insecure housing, immigration concerns, emotional attachment or fear that no one will believe them. Leaving or reporting may temporarily increase risk in some situations. The safest next action is individual and should not be prescribed by an untrained person. [2, 4]

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Why leaving or reporting may be difficult
text: Avoid asking “Why didn’t you leave?” A better question is: “What would feel most helpful and safe for you right now?”

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Supporting someone who discloses abuse
text: WHO describes the LIVES approach for first-line support: Listen, Inquire about needs, Validate, Enhance safety and Support. In non-clinical settings, this is best used as an orientation to compassionate responses, not as permission to perform clinical risk assessments or investigations. [4, 5]

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Supporting someone who discloses abuse
text: “Thank you for telling me.” “You deserve to be treated with respect.” “You do not have to tell me more than you want to.” “Would you like information about confidential support options and any limits to confidentiality?”

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Confidentiality, privacy and safeguarding
text: Ask whether it is safe to call, text or leave messages. Do not assume that a phone or internet account is private. Avoid storing names, details or screenshots without a legitimate reason, a secure process and informed consent. Do not share a survivor’s story with family, community leaders or social media contacts. Explain any relevant mandatory reporting, child-protection or imminent-danger exceptions before inviting sensitive disclosure.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Confidentiality, privacy and safeguarding
text: For children, involve trained safeguarding personnel using age-appropriate procedures and applicable local rules. Do not promise absolute secrecy. Where there is a clear immediate threat, prioritise urgent protection and professional assistance.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Rwanda-specific support and referral
text: Rwanda’s Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion describes Isange One Stop Centres as coordinated entry points providing healthcare, psychosocial support, justice-related services and referral to shelter when needed. UNHCR Rwanda also provides information about service access. [6, 7]

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Rwanda-specific support and referral
text: Important: UNHCR cautions that approaching an Isange Centre may result in the incident being reported to law-enforcement authorities. Explain this possibility before a survivor shares identifiable information and confirm local confidentiality and reporting processes with qualified personnel. These contacts do not guarantee an immediate answer or suitability in every situation. [7]

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Rwanda-specific support and referral
text: Offer the person the option to contact a verified service privately and discuss transport, accessibility or communication barriers. Do not make a formal report on an adult survivor’s behalf without understanding the relevant law, safety implications and consent, except where applicable legal or safeguarding duties require action.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 1 — A university student and constant monitoring
text: Fictional case: A university student in Kigali receives dozens of messages each day from a dating partner asking for location updates. When the student attends a study group, the partner calls repeatedly, insults the student and threatens to post private messages online. The student begins withdrawing from classmates to avoid conflict.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 1 — A university student and constant monitoring
text: Learning discussion: What patterns are concerning? Repeated monitoring, humiliation, threats and isolation suggest coercive control. What would be unsafe? Instructing the student to confront the partner immediately or change phone settings without assessing the risk. What might help? Private, nonjudgmental support and information about trusted services.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 2 — Humiliation at work
text: Fictional case: A supervisor repeatedly tells a female employee she is incapable of leadership because of her gender, insults her during meetings and threatens her promotion if she complains. A colleague wants to help but is worried about retaliation.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 2 — Humiliation at work
text: Learning discussion: The gender-based insults, threats and unequal power are important. The colleague could ask privately whether support is welcome, avoid circulating the story, and offer information about independent workplace reporting or specialist services. The colleague should not promise that reporting will be risk-free.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 3 — Family pressure and isolation
text: Fictional case: A married adult in Musanze is regularly told that speaking to relatives is a betrayal. Their partner controls access to transport money and threatens to remove contact with the children if the adult seeks advice.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 3 — Family pressure and isolation
text: Learning discussion: Multiple behaviors—social isolation, threats and financial restriction—may work together. The affected adult’s priorities and safety should guide any referral. Pressuring immediate separation could increase danger.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 4 — Digital humiliation
text: Fictional case: A former partner sends insulting messages, creates fake accounts and threatens to publish private information. Friends suggest responding publicly with screenshots, but the person feels unsafe.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 4 — Digital humiliation
text: Learning discussion: Online harassment and threats can be forms of emotional abuse. Public retaliation may intensify harassment. Appropriate options depend on safety, available support and local procedures. A specialist can help consider documentation and reporting without exposing sensitive information unnecessarily.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 5 — A child who hears repeated threats
text: Fictional case: A young adolescent hears one caregiver threaten another and repeatedly witnesses humiliation at home. The child becomes worried about going home and has difficulty concentrating at school.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Scenario 5 — A child who hears repeated threats
text: Learning discussion: The child’s distress is important even without direct physical assault. A responsible adult should follow established safeguarding procedures, avoid asking the child to investigate or mediate, and seek support from appropriate child protection professionals.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Reflection without disclosure
text: A learner may reflect privately or choose not to answer. Collecting identifiable disclosures is not necessary for this exercise.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Glossary
text: Emotional abuse: Behavior that undermines emotional wellbeing through degradation, threats, manipulation or other harmful treatment. Psychological abuse: Abusive behavior that creates fear, distress or coercion, including nonverbal control.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Glossary
text: Verbal abuse: Insults, degrading language, threats or humiliating speech used to harm or control.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Glossary
text: Coercive control: A pattern of behaviors that limits choices and independence.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Glossary
text: Survivor-centred: An approach prioritizing safety, dignity, informed choices and individual needs.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Glossary
text: Safeguarding: Procedures to protect people, especially children and at-risk people, from harm.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Glossary
text: Referral: Connecting a person to an appropriate qualified service according to need and safety.

title: Emotional, Psychological and Verbal Abuse — Publication and review checklist
text: Evidence-informed educational material only. No claim of professional clinical, legal or safeguarding approval has been made. Review the entire chapter before publishing or adapting it for an AI chatbot or public awareness campaign.
