title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Understanding economic violence
text: Economic violence or economic abuse occurs when a person uses money, employment, property, debt, education, benefits, or access to resources to control, exploit, or harm another person. Financial abuse is often used for direct control of income, accounts, assets, and spending; economic abuse is wider and can also undermine a person's ability to obtain or keep resources. It can occur in intimate relationships, families, care arrangements, and other settings. [1, 2]

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Understanding economic violence
text: The central concern is not whether partners share an account or earn different amounts. It is whether someone uses threats, deception, intimidation, coercion, or unequal power to deny another person genuine choice and access to necessary resources. A single incident can be serious, while some abuse develops as a repeated pattern.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Understanding economic violence
text: Key principle: Having less income, depending on family members, or choosing to share finances does not itself mean abuse. Control, coercion, exploitation, and the person's freedom to make decisions are critical to understanding the situation.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Why economic abuse matters
text: Economic abuse can make it harder to afford food, medication, transport, safe housing, school fees, or communication. It can undermine financial independence, interrupt education or employment, create debt, and make asking for help or leaving an abusive situation more difficult. These barriers can continue after a relationship ends. [2, 3]

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Why economic abuse matters
text: Economic abuse may occur together with emotional, physical, sexual, or technology-facilitated abuse.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Why economic abuse matters
text: The presence of economic abuse does not establish that all other types are present, but it should prompt careful attention to the person's safety and choices.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Forms of economic violence
text: A controlling person may keep all income, refuse access to funds for necessary food or treatment, require receipts for every small purchase as a form of surveillance, confiscate earnings, or deny money for transport to seek help. Restrictions can become especially harmful when a person has children, a disability, or health-related needs.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Forms of economic violence
text: This can include taking savings, livestock, land-related proceeds, inventory, or personal possessions without agreement; using another person's bank or mobile-money account without permission; pressuring someone to transfer property; or diverting income from a jointly run business. The exact legal classification depends on the circumstances and applicable Rwandan law.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Forms of economic violence
text: An abusive person may forbid employment or schooling, repeatedly interrupt work, damage tools, interfere with a job interview, refuse reasonable childcare arrangements as a tactic of control, or harass someone at their workplace until they lose opportunities. Sabotage can make long-term independence harder.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Forms of economic violence
text: Someone may be pressured to borrow money, become a guarantor, hand over a PIN, sign a contract they do not understand, or accept liability for another person's purchases. A debt may become a mechanism of control when consent is obtained through threats or deception. A person should be able to seek an independent explanation before making a financial commitment.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Forms of economic violence
text: Digital economic abuse may involve monitoring mobile-money messages, demanding wallet or banking PINs, accessing online accounts, requiring location-sharing to authorize purchases, or using shared devices to track transactions. Changing access on a monitored device can sometimes alert an abusive person, so digital safety should be considered before acting.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Forms of economic violence
text: A family member or caregiver might control an older person's funds, disability-related resources, pension, or essential belongings. Economic abuse can affect people of any gender and age. Child safeguarding and other legal duties may apply when a child or dependent person is involved.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Financial partnership versus financial control
text: Healthy collaboration: Partners may voluntarily choose a shared budget, discuss priorities, give one person responsibility for paying bills, or agree to save for a business. Each person can ask questions, understand important decisions, raise concerns without fear, and seek access to necessities.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Financial partnership versus financial control
text: Concerning control: One partner threatens punishment for asking about finances, takes earnings without permission, insists on secrecy, prevents work, or uses access to basic necessities to force compliance. What matters is the power dynamic and freedom to disagree, not simply the household accounting arrangement. [1, 3]

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Warning signs and patterns
text: These signs invite careful reflection rather than automatic diagnosis of a relationship. A single checklist cannot determine a person's risk. A trained GBV professional can help explore what is happening in context.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Causes, power dynamics, and misconceptions
text: Economic abuse is linked to unequal power, controlling attitudes, gender norms, and opportunities for exploitation. Poverty or unemployment may increase practical vulnerability, but they do not excuse abuse. A person who experiences financial dependence is not responsible for another person's controlling behavior. [4]

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Causes, power dynamics, and misconceptions
text: Myth: Only wealthy people can experience financial abuse. Fact: Control can involve any amount of money or resources.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Causes, power dynamics, and misconceptions
text: Myth: If one partner earns the money, they are entitled to control all decisions. Fact: Income differences do not justify coercion or denial of dignity.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Causes, power dynamics, and misconceptions
text: Myth: Economic abuse ends once people separate. Fact: Property disputes, debt, employment disruption, and digital access may continue to affect survivors.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Effects on wellbeing and opportunities
text: Possible effects include chronic stress, fear, loss of confidence, sleep problems, limited mobility, disrupted healthcare, interrupted schooling, job loss, food insecurity, housing instability, and difficulty rebuilding savings. The effects vary between individuals, and some people maintain important sources of strength and support despite abuse. [2, 3, 4]

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Effects on wellbeing and opportunities
text: Children may be affected when economic coercion reduces access to basic needs or creates unsafe family conditions. Responding appropriately can require coordinated attention to social support, healthcare, education, and legal safeguards.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Survivor-centred first response
text: A supportive person should listen without judgment, acknowledge what has been shared, ask about immediate needs without demanding details, and offer choices rather than directives. Do not tell the person to confront an abuser, leave immediately, take money, expose records publicly, or disclose passwords. Such actions can increase danger in some situations.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Survivor-centred first response
text: Ask whether the conversation, device, and location are safe. Explain privacy and mandatory-reporting limits accurately. If specialized services are available, offer to help the person contact them in a way they choose. WHO's survivor-centred care principles prioritize listening, inquiry about needs, validation, safety, and support. [4, 5]

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Financial safety: choice-based considerations
text: Financial safety planning should be individualized with a qualified GBV professional where possible. A person may consider the safety of identity documents, account access, emergency transportation, essential medication, business documents, and trusted contacts. The safest choices depend on monitoring, threats, dependents, and available resources. [3]

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Financial safety: choice-based considerations
text: Immediate safety: If someone is in immediate danger, seek urgent help from an appropriate local emergency or protection service. This chapter cannot assess an individual's risk or replace specialist safety planning.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Facilitator notes and safeguarding
text: For group education, avoid asking participants to disclose personal experiences. Use fictional cases, allow people to pass, do not collect names or financial information during exercises, and provide private referral options. Do not promise that group discussions are confidential. Facilitators should know how to respond if someone reports immediate danger or a child-safeguarding concern.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Facilitator notes and safeguarding
text: Rwanda-specific terminology, property and family-law statements, workplace rights, financial-service procedures, and referral contacts must be checked by local GBV/legal professionals before publication.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Facilitator notes and safeguarding
text: Any digital version should minimize data collection and provide a safe exit option.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Accessing support in Rwanda
text: MIGEPROF describes Isange One Stop Centres as providing coordinated healthcare, psychosocial support, legal and protection services. UNHCR Rwanda lists the Isange toll-free contact as 3029 and notes that contacting a centre may result in a report to law enforcement. MIGEPROF also lists RIB 116 / 3512, Gender Monitoring Office 5798, and MIGEPROF 9059. Contact details and service arrangements should be rechecked before public dissemination. [6, 7]

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Accessing support in Rwanda
text: If a person is seeking assistance with property, contracts, debt, or employment disputes, a verified Rwandan legal-aid provider or appropriate local institution should explain applicable rights. No outcome can be guaranteed from this general educational material.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Glossary
text: Economic abuse: Using resources or economic opportunities to control, exploit, or harm a person.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Glossary
text: Financial abuse: Misuse or control of money, accounts, property, and financial decisions.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Glossary
text: Employment sabotage: Interfering with a person's opportunity to obtain or maintain work.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Glossary
text: Economic exploitation: Taking or using another person's financial resources or labor through coercion or misuse of power.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Glossary
text: Coercive control: A pattern of conduct that restricts another person's independence through intimidation, threats, or other controlling tactics.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Glossary
text: Survivor-centred support: Support that prioritizes the person's dignity, safety, informed choice, and needs.

title: Economic Violence and Financial Control — Glossary
text: Digital financial safety: Considering risks from monitored devices, payment accounts, messages, and transaction information.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — What is technology-facilitated GBV?
text: Technology-facilitated gender-based violence is a harmful act that is committed, enabled, intensified, or spread through information and communication technology and connected to gender-based targeting or power inequalities. It can cause psychological, sexual, social, economic, political, or physical harm. It may occur through phones, messages, social media, email, shared cloud accounts, smart devices, gaming platforms, or location tools. [1, 2]

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — What is technology-facilitated GBV?
text: The word "online" captures only part of the problem. A person may be monitored through location settings, harassed by telephone, tracked through shared accounts, or threatened with the release of private information. Digital harm can cross into offline life when a location is exposed, an employer is contacted, or threats create fear of physical assault.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — What is technology-facilitated GBV?
text: Not every rude online comment is necessarily GBV. Context matters: discriminatory targeting, sexualized threats, controlling behavior, repeated harassment, and misuse of power can signal gender-based abuse. Even where a single act is not clearly categorized as GBV, it may still be harmful and merit support.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — How digital abuse differs from ordinary disagreement
text: Disagreement involves expressing a different view. Abuse uses intimidation, non-consensual exposure, threats, deception, repeated unwanted contact, or coercion to cause harm or restrict another person's freedom. The affected person does not need to prove a repeated pattern before a serious threat or non-consensual intimate-image disclosure is taken seriously.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — How digital abuse differs from ordinary disagreement
text: The scale and speed of digital distribution can multiply harm: material can be copied rapidly, resurface after removal, be shared anonymously, or reach workplaces and families. Yet digital risks should not be presented as unavoidable; platforms, schools, employers, public institutions and other actors have responsibilities to prevent and respond.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Major forms of technology-facilitated abuse
text: Repeated insulting, sexualized, degrading, or threatening messages, including coordinated attacks intended to shame or silence a person. A single credible threat is serious even without repetition.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Major forms of technology-facilitated abuse
text: Persistent unwanted messages, tracking, repeated account contact, checking whereabouts, or using shared digital services to monitor someone. It may accompany intimate partner violence.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Major forms of technology-facilitated abuse
text: Sharing, threatening to share, or creating intimate images without the person's agreement, including synthetic or manipulated material. Prior consensual creation or sharing with one person never means consent to redistribution.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Major forms of technology-facilitated abuse
text: Publishing a home address, telephone number, private correspondence, or identifying details to expose someone to threats, harassment, or loss of safety.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Major forms of technology-facilitated abuse
text: Creating a false profile, pretending to be someone else, accessing their accounts without authorization, or posting messages in their name to intimidate, defraud, or damage relationships.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Major forms of technology-facilitated abuse
text: Demanding sexual images, sexual acts, money, or compliance by threatening to release private material or harm someone. A survivor is not responsible for the threat.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Major forms of technology-facilitated abuse
text: Using shared accounts, connected devices, permissions, location services, or potentially malicious tools to track movements or communications without informed agreement.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Major forms of technology-facilitated abuse
text: Restricting access to mobile money, digital work platforms or education accounts; contacting employers with threats; or using account control to interfere with income or study.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Why forms of abuse overlap
text: A former partner might monitor a shared cloud account, send threats, impersonate a survivor online, and contact their workplace. The harm is not only "a password problem" or "a social media problem"; it may be part of broader coercive control. Responses should consider immediate safety, relationships of power, technology access, the survivor's preferences, and available support.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — The role of artificial intelligence
text: AI tools can be misused to create fabricated intimate images, impersonate voices, produce believable forged messages, or amplify targeted abuse. A manipulated image is not proof that an event occurred. If a person is targeted, responders should avoid sharing the material further, blaming the survivor, or making promises that removal from the internet will be complete. [1, 3]

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — The role of artificial intelligence
text: Prevention also requires platforms and institutions to address reporting failures, abusive content dissemination, privacy weaknesses, and harmful design practices. The burden should not be placed entirely on the targeted person.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Risk factors and unequal exposure
text: Women and girls are disproportionately exposed to many forms of technology-facilitated violence; public-facing women, journalists, women in leadership, and people experiencing discrimination can face targeted attacks. Children and adolescents have distinct developmental and protection needs. Individuals with disabilities or limited digital access may face extra obstacles to safe reporting. [1, 2]

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Risk factors and unequal exposure
text: Risk factors do not predict who will be abused and do not excuse perpetrators. A person should never be blamed for using social media, posting photographs, entering a relationship, trusting somebody, or having limited technical knowledge.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Signs that digital behavior is becoming unsafe
text: These signs are not proof of surveillance or wrongdoing by a particular person. Some account anomalies have ordinary technical explanations. Seek knowledgeable assistance without making risky assumptions or confronting a suspected abuser.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Impact on wellbeing, rights and participation
text: Digital abuse may cause fear, sleep problems, shame, anxiety, concentration difficulties, social isolation, or avoidance of digital spaces. It can also disrupt school, work, income, relationships, and civic participation. These responses are understandable and vary by person. No one should need to provide intimate details in order to receive empathy and basic information.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Impact on wellbeing, rights and participation
text: Some people experience threats to physical safety, particularly when location details are disclosed or an abusive person has access to devices. Psychological support and digital-security assistance can complement, rather than replace, appropriate medical, legal, or protection services.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — First response: safety before technology
text: If someone discloses digital abuse, ask whether it is safe to discuss the issue on the current device or channel. Listen calmly, avoid requesting screenshots or intimate images, and ask what the person wants help with. Do not pressure them to report, block, change a password, or confront someone immediately. They may be using a monitored device. [4]

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — First response: safety before technology
text: 1. Check immediate physical and communication safety. 2. Ask what support is wanted. 3. Consider whether accounts/devices may be monitored. 4. Discuss practical options without imposing them.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — First response: safety before technology
text: 5. Offer verified GBV, legal, protection or cybersecurity support. 6. Record only information necessary for a safe referral.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Privacy and account-security options
text: Where it is safe, a trusted specialist may help review account recovery information, active sessions, login alerts, privacy and sharing permissions, connected devices, cloud photo synchronization, location sharing, and two-factor authentication. Separate accounts and unique passwords can reduce some risks, but changing them may notify another person or lock the survivor out of essential services.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Privacy and account-security options
text: When technology may be monitored, using a separate trusted device or seeking discreet specialist support can be safer than investigating the suspected device. Avoid installing unknown "anti-spyware" products or attempting to hack another account. Technical checks should be informed by consent, professional competence, and local law.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Evidence and incident documentation
text: If safe and desired, documenting dates, platforms, usernames, links, messages and threats may help a report. Evidence can be stored through a trusted, secure method, but creating or retaining files may also expose someone if their device is monitored. A survivor can ask a qualified provider how to document material without causing additional harm.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Evidence and incident documentation
text: Do not forward intimate content in group chats or to VUGA NDAKUMVA staff simply to "prove" a case. Where a child may be depicted in sexual content, do not download, copy, or redistribute it; seek prompt advice from child protection or law enforcement channels on how to report the content safely.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Blocking, reporting and removing content
text: Platforms may offer blocking, muting, account-reporting, impersonation reporting, and requests to remove private or intimate content. These tools may reduce exposure but do not guarantee removal or safety. Blocking or reporting can sometimes trigger retaliation; consider timing and safety before acting. Avoid communicating directly with an extortionist without specialist advice.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Blocking, reporting and removing content
text: If a person is being blackmailed, remind them they did not cause the abuse. Paying money or providing further material does not reliably end extortion. Specialist support can help identify safer next actions.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Responding to children and adolescents
text: Online grooming, sexual extortion, image-based abuse, and harassment involving children require age-appropriate safeguarding. Adults should respond without blame, use developmentally appropriate language, and avoid unnecessary repeated questioning. Confidentiality limits and mandatory reporting duties must be explained in a manner appropriate to the child and local law. [2]

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Responding to children and adolescents
text: A child should not be asked to negotiate with a suspected perpetrator. If there is imminent danger or sexual exploitation, contact an appropriate protection or emergency service. School staff should follow vetted safeguarding protocols rather than handling the matter through informal public discussion.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — What families, schools and workplaces can do
text: Prevention includes clear rules against harassment; private and accessible reporting pathways; trained focal points; proportional institutional responses; digital literacy; and policies that protect survivors against retaliation. Staff should not force a survivor to confront an alleged perpetrator or expose private evidence publicly.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — What families, schools and workplaces can do
text: Families can normalize asking permission before sharing photos and discussing account privacy without using fear. Schools can teach respectful digital communication and enable confidential referrals. Employers can protect work credentials and document harassment without punishing the person experiencing it.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Rwanda: where to seek support
text: Rwanda's Isange One Stop Centres provide integrated GBV-related services. RIB publishes the following contacts: 3029 for Isange One Stop Centre, 3512 for domestic and gender-based violence reporting, 116 for child abuse, and 166 for emergencies or crime-related information. These are published contacts, not a guarantee that every digital complaint can be handled through every line. [5, 6]

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Rwanda: where to seek support
text: UNHCR Rwanda notes that approaching an Isange Centre may lead to law-enforcement reporting. Where privacy or reporting obligations could affect safety, ask service providers to explain confidentiality limits and available options before disclosing sensitive details. For urgent physical danger, use emergency assistance and consider a safe location rather than relying only on online platform reports. [6]

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Glossary
text: Cyberstalking: Repeated unwanted following, contact or monitoring facilitated by technology.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Glossary
text: Doxing: Revealing private or identifying information without authorization, often to expose someone to harm.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Glossary
text: Image-based abuse: Non-consensual creation, sharing or threatening to share intimate imagery, including manipulated images.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Glossary
text: Impersonation: Pretending to be another person online to mislead or harm others.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Glossary
text: Digital coercive control: Using digital access, communications or monitoring to restrict a person's freedom.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Glossary
text: Safeguarding: Actions and responsibilities intended to prevent and respond to harm, especially involving children or vulnerable people.

title: Technology-Facilitated and Online Gender-Based Violence — Glossary
text: Two-factor authentication: An additional verification step to access an account; useful but must be deployed safely.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Understanding violence against children and adolescents
text: Gender-based violence (GBV) includes harmful acts rooted in gender-related power differences, discrimination, or expectations. Children and adolescents can experience sexual abuse, harassment, exploitation, forced or coerced relationships, emotional intimidation, and violence in the home, school or digital environment. Other forms of violence against children may not be gender-based; nevertheless, all children need protection.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Understanding violence against children and adolescents
text: The term child generally refers to a person below 18 years in international child-rights frameworks. Adolescence overlaps with childhood; young people have developing decision-making abilities and increasing autonomy, while adults and institutions retain responsibilities to protect them. Protective responses should respect a young person’s dignity, voice, development and safety.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Understanding violence against children and adolescents
text: GBV can affect girls and boys, including children with disabilities and children who are socially excluded. Girls may face distinctive gendered risks, but no child should be overlooked because of sex, gender, background, disability or perceived identity.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — What forms of GBV can affect children?
text: These categories may overlap. A teacher who uses grades to demand a sexual favor combines abuse of authority, exploitation and harassment. The label matters less than recognizing harm and connecting the child with safe help.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Where abuse may occur
text: Risk can arise within families and extended households, schools and boarding settings, sports or religious activities, workplaces involving young people, transportation, camps, service institutions and online spaces. Abuse may be perpetrated by someone known and trusted, not only by strangers. Familiarity and social status must never replace safeguarding checks.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Power, dependence and age-appropriate consent
text: Children deserve to have their views heard and to understand choices affecting them. Yet a child’s apparent compliance, silence, receipt of gifts, or previous friendliness must not be treated as consent to sexual abuse. Significant age, authority and dependence may make refusal unsafe or meaningful agreement impossible. Applicable national law determines legal age thresholds and offences; this educational chapter does not give an exhaustive statement of Rwandan legal requirements.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Power, dependence and age-appropriate consent
text: For healthy daily interactions, children can learn that they may express discomfort, say no to unwanted contact, ask questions before sharing personal information, and seek help from safe adults. Such lessons never transfer responsibility for preventing abuse from adults to children.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Grooming and manipulation
text: Grooming involves gaining a child’s trust, access, secrecy or dependence to facilitate exploitation. It may involve excessive gifts, special treatment, isolating a young person, requesting private conversations, testing boundaries or using fear and threats. None of these behaviors alone proves grooming; patterns and context matter.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Grooming and manipulation
text: Adults should be alert to boundary violations without teaching that every caring adult is dangerous. A useful school or community rule is that safeguarding relationships remain transparent, appropriately supervised and accountable.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Early warning signs: notice, do not diagnose
text: Some children experiencing abuse may show sudden fear of a particular person or place; changes in sleep, appetite, school attendance or concentration; withdrawal; distress after online contact; unexplained gifts or money; or injuries. Others show few outward signs. These changes have many possible causes, so the correct action is a calm, non-accusatory check-in and consultation with an appropriate safeguarding professional, not an assumption that abuse has occurred.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Early warning signs: notice, do not diagnose
text: Avoid turning warning-sign checklists into public screening tools or asking a child to reveal traumatic details in a group setting.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Effects on health, learning and development
text: Violence may affect physical safety, sexual and reproductive health, emotional wellbeing, sleep, trust, school participation, social connection and long-term health. Responses vary; some children may recover with timely support, while others need sustained medical, psychosocial, educational or protection services. Do not tell a child that they will inevitably be permanently damaged.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Effects on health, learning and development
text: Support should address practical needs such as safe transport, school continuity, a trusted non-offending caregiver, communication needs, accessibility and freedom from retaliation as well as emotional distress.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Safe first response when a child tells you about abuse
text: The first adult response can shape whether a child receives help. Use calm, simple, nonjudgmental language. Listen, thank the child for telling you, affirm that the harm is not their responsibility, and explain what will happen next using age-appropriate words.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Safe first response when a child tells you about abuse
text: Specialist interviews, medical examinations and evidence handling should be performed by appropriately trained professionals following child-protection procedures.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Confidentiality and safeguarding responsibilities
text: Confidentiality is important, but it is not absolute when a child may need protection or reporting is legally required. Before asking for sensitive details, describe the limits of privacy in language the young person can understand. Share information only with authorized people who need it for safety and care. Keep records minimal, secure, accurate and factual; do not circulate images or allegations in messaging groups.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Confidentiality and safeguarding responsibilities
text: Organizations must verify the current Rwandan reporting rules, the relevant authorities, age-related consent and assent requirements, and internal escalation routes with qualified local legal and child-protection experts. When a caregiver may be responsible for harm, do not automatically send the child back to that caregiver without a safety assessment.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Urgent health needs after sexual assault
text: A child or adolescent who may have experienced recent sexual assault should be offered prompt evaluation by trained healthcare personnel, even without visible injuries. Emergency care can address injuries, sexually transmitted infections, psychological support and, where appropriate, time-sensitive prevention.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Urgent health needs after sexual assault
text: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): WHO advises assessing and offering PEP when clinically indicated, as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after relevant exposure. Emergency contraception: WHO guidance describes offering it to eligible girls after rape as soon as possible, within 120 hours (five days), when appropriate. These are clinical decisions for trained providers; the handbook does not instruct readers to self-medicate. A child who comes for help after these time windows still needs and deserves healthcare, protection and psychosocial support. Do not withhold care because evidence was not preserved or because the family has not made a police report.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Safer school and youth-program responses
text: Schools and organizations should adopt clear staff conduct rules, an accessible reporting route, trusted designated safeguarding leads, safe transportation and supervision policies, and a prohibition on retaliation. Reporting arrangements must work for children with disabilities and for children who do not speak the primary school language fluently.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Safer school and youth-program responses
text: Educators should teach respectful relationships, non-discrimination, consent-related body safety and digital skills without asking students to share personal histories. A teacher receiving a disclosure should follow the safeguarding process rather than conduct a private investigation.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Online grooming, harassment and image-based abuse
text: Digital abuse may involve persistent sexual messages, pressure for intimate images, pretending to be a peer, threatening to disclose private material, impersonation or location tracking. Even if an adolescent voluntarily sent an image, threats and non-consensual distribution are not justified. Never blame the young person or ask them to forward intimate material to an educator or chatbot.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Online grooming, harassment and image-based abuse
text: If an offender can access the child’s phone or accounts, sudden changes to passwords or settings may create additional danger. Seek help from a trusted safeguarding or digital-safety professional and use a safe device when possible. Platforms may offer abuse-reporting options, but reports should be made with attention to child safety and local procedures.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Prevention: family, community and institutions
text: The WHO/UNICEF INSPIRE framework identifies seven complementary strategies: implementing and enforcing laws; changing harmful norms and values; creating safe environments; supporting parents and caregivers; strengthening household income and economic security; providing response and support services; and improving education and life skills. Child protection cannot be achieved by putting all responsibility on individual children.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Prevention: family, community and institutions
text: At home, caregivers can use respectful communication, nonviolent discipline, predictable support and age-appropriate discussions about boundaries. In the community, leaders can challenge narratives that blame survivors or shield powerful adults. Institutions should create accountable reporting channels and transparent procedures.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Access to support in Rwanda
text: Rwanda’s Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion (MIGEPROF) describes Isange One Stop Centres as providing coordinated healthcare, psychosocial, justice and protection services for GBV and child abuse. UNHCR Rwanda lists the Isange toll-free number as 3029. MIGEPROF publishes 711 for the National Child Development Agency (NCDA) and 116 / 3512 for the Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB). Availability and suitability should be checked at the time of use.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Access to support in Rwanda
text: UNHCR notes that approaching an Isange Centre may result in a report to law enforcement. Before sharing sensitive details, seek an explanation of privacy, safeguarding and reporting requirements. If a child is in immediate danger, contact an appropriate emergency or child-protection service without delay.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Supporting different needs
text: A child with a disability may need a qualified interpreter, accessible transport, visual communication or more time to express concerns. Avoid relying on a suspected offender as an interpreter or caregiver during a disclosure. Children in displacement, migration, institutional care or severe economic hardship may need integrated practical support. All children should be treated with equal dignity.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Key terms
text: Child safeguarding: Organizational and professional duties to prevent and respond to harm against children.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Key terms
text: Disclosure: When someone communicates information or concerns about abuse.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Key terms
text: Grooming: A pattern of manipulation and boundary crossing intended to facilitate exploitation.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Key terms
text: Coercion: Pressure, intimidation, threats or misuse of power that undermines free choice.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Key terms
text: Non-offending caregiver: A caregiver not implicated in the harm who can support safe care.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Key terms
text: Trauma-informed care: An approach that prioritizes physical and emotional safety, dignity, choice and avoiding re-traumatization.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Key terms
text: PEP: Time-sensitive medication prescribed by a clinician after qualifying HIV exposure.

title: Gender-Based Violence Against Children and Adolescents — Key terms
text: Referral pathway: An agreed process for connecting someone with appropriate specialist support.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Start here: What will you learn?
text: Alcohol and other psychoactive substances can change how the brain and body work. Understanding the basics helps people make informed decisions, notice risks, support others and seek appropriate care. This lesson explains the meaning of alcohol and drugs without blame or frightening exaggeration.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Start here: What will you learn?
text: Estimated learning time: about 8–12 minutes for the core text; optional activities can be completed separately. This is a design estimate, not a measured completion time.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Start here: What will you learn?
text: How to use this lesson: Read the essential explanation first. If you prefer, skip activities and go directly to Key Takeaways or Get Help. Future audio, video and visual formats must offer an equivalent text alternative.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Start here: What will you learn?
text: For teachers and caregivers: Explain concepts without assuming a young person has already used substances. Avoid public disclosures and use fictional examples instead.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — What is alcohol?
text: Alcoholic drinks contain ethanol. Ethanol is a psychoactive chemical, meaning it affects the brain and can change judgment, attention, mood, coordination and behavior. It is also toxic: alcohol consumption can damage health and, for some people, lead to dependence. Beer, wine and spirits differ in strength and serving size, but the psychoactive ingredient is ethanol. [1]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — What is alcohol?
text: Someone may drink alcohol in a social setting and appear relaxed, but alcohol can still impair reaction time or decision-making. Harm is not limited to people with dependence. Risk can occur after a single occasion, over repeated use, or through long-term health effects. Even low consumption is not risk-free. [1]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — What is alcohol?
text: A key distinction: alcohol is socially familiar in many settings, but common does not mean harmless. Alcohol is classified among psychoactive substances, even when it is legally sold to adults under applicable laws. [1,2]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — What is alcohol?
text: Example: A person leaves a celebration after drinking and feels confident enough to ride a motorcycle. Their confidence does not mean their reaction time is unaffected. The safer choice is not to drive or ride while impaired.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — What are drugs and psychoactive substances?
text: In healthcare, the word drug can mean a medicine used to prevent or treat illness. In everyday conversation, it often refers to substances used for non-medical effects. These meanings are not identical. A psychoactive substance affects mental processes such as perception, thinking, feelings, awareness or behavior. Alcohol, nicotine, some prescribed medicines, cannabis, opioids and stimulants can be psychoactive. [2,3]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — What are drugs and psychoactive substances?
text: Not every medicine is psychoactive, and not every psychoactive substance automatically causes dependence. Some medicines are effective and important when appropriately prescribed and used; they may also carry risks if misused. Legal status, medical usefulness and health risk are different questions. [2,3]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — What are drugs and psychoactive substances?
text: Rather than labeling people as “good” or “bad,” this programme uses neutral, accurate terms such as substance use, harmful use and substance use disorder.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Broad substance groups: a practical guide
text: Different substances work differently. The categories below are simplified for education; many substances have mixed effects, and the same substance can affect people differently.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Broad substance groups: a practical guide
text: These examples describe categories; they are not instructions for use. Avoid assuming a product is safe because it is “natural,” prescribed to someone else, or legally available. [2,3]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — How can substances affect the body and brain?
text: Psychoactive substances can influence communication between nerve cells and alter processes involved in attention, pleasure, movement, memory, sleep or emotions. The exact mechanism and level of risk depend on the substance, amount, individual health, circumstances and whether other substances are involved. [2,3]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — How can substances affect the body and brain?
text: Short-term concerns can include impaired decisions, falls, injuries, confusion, unsafe driving, or poisoning. Longer-term concerns may include worsening physical health, problems in relationships or work, and substance use disorders. Not everyone who uses a substance develops a disorder, but adverse effects can happen without a diagnosis. [1,3]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — How can substances affect the body and brain?
text: Some medications can interact with alcohol or other substances. A pharmacist or clinician can advise on prescribed medicines; a learning website should not attempt individualized interaction checks.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Three ideas that are often confused
text: Avoid conclusions based on appearances, social stereotypes, or a single behavior. A person concerned about their use can seek a confidential professional assessment. [4]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Myths versus facts
text: Language matters: use “person experiencing a substance use disorder” instead of labels that reduce an individual to their condition.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Interactive learning: choose and learn
text: These are website interaction scripts presented in readable PDF form. Users will tap an option and receive feedback in the eventual application. No answer will be treated as a diagnosis; no personal information is requested.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — When a situation needs urgent care
text: Seek urgent medical assistance if a person is unconscious, cannot be awakened, has dangerously slow or irregular breathing, experiences seizures, or shows other serious signs of poisoning. Contact the appropriate emergency service or reach an emergency department immediately. Do not leave an unresponsive person alone while arranging help.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — When a situation needs urgent care
text: If a person may be dependent on alcohol and is considering suddenly stopping, they should discuss withdrawal risk with a qualified clinician. Alcohol withdrawal can be medically dangerous and sometimes requires supervised care. This lesson is not a detoxification guide.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — When a situation needs urgent care
text: If you are supporting a young person, prioritize their immediate safety and connect them with a trusted, appropriate adult or qualified professional. Avoid public disclosure or punitive humiliation.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — When a situation needs urgent care
text: Rwanda-specific emergency numbers and referral services must be independently verified and approved before the platform publishes them. The educational lesson does not invent an emergency contact.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — When a situation needs urgent care
text: This lesson does not provide medication, dosing, substance preparation, detoxification instructions or individualized medical advice.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — A simple way to support someone
text: A helpful conversation can begin with specific, nonjudgmental observations: “I noticed you have seemed unwell lately, and I am concerned. Would you like to talk?” Listen, ask what support they want, and avoid threats or public accusations. Offer help finding professional assessment if needed. Do not promise secrecy when a child or another person is at immediate risk.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — A simple way to support someone
text: For adults: support does not mean controlling their every decision. For children: safeguarding obligations and age-appropriate family or professional involvement may apply.

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Key takeaways
text: 1. Alcohol is a psychoactive, toxic substance containing ethanol. [1]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Key takeaways
text: 2. Drugs may refer to legitimate medicines or substances used for non-medical effects; context matters. [2,3]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Key takeaways
text: 3. Legal availability does not prove safety, and not every psychoactive substance causes dependence. [2]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Key takeaways
text: 4. Substance use, health risks and substance use disorders are related but distinct concepts. [1,4]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Key takeaways
text: 5. People deserve respectful information and access to professional care without shame. [4]

title: What Are Alcohol and Drugs? — Key takeaways
text: What next? Explore the next lesson in “Understanding Alcohol & Drugs,” or open “Get Help & Support Someone.” No assessment is required to continue.

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Start with the big idea
text: Learning objectives: After this topic, a learner should be able to explain how substances reach and affect the brain; identify key body systems that can be affected; distinguish short-term effects from long-term harm; recognize risk differences; and identify symptoms needing urgent assistance.

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Start with the big idea
text: Alcohol and other psychoactive substances affect the body because their molecules interact with cells and biological systems. Many substances influence the brain, changing alertness, judgment, memory, movement, mood or pain perception. They may also affect breathing, the heart, liver, digestive system and other organs. Effects depend on the particular substance and the person’s circumstances. [1-5]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Start with the big idea
text: The risk is not the same for every substance, dose, person, or setting. This lesson describes patterns rather than predicting what will happen to an individual.

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Start with the big idea
text: A fictional adult drinks alcohol at a celebration and feels confident and talkative. Their sense of confidence does not prove that their balance, reaction time, or driving ability is intact. This illustrates how subjective feelings and actual performance can differ.

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — What happens in the brain?
text: The brain consists of billions of nerve cells, called neurons. They communicate using electrical activity and chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. Substances can change how chemical signals are released, received, or cleared. These changes can influence attention, emotions, pain, movement, sleep, memory and behavior. [2,3]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — What happens in the brain?
text: Dopamine helps the brain learn from rewards and cues. Some substances strongly reinforce repeated use through reward-related circuits. However, addiction is not simply “too much dopamine.” It involves multiple brain systems, learning processes, environment, biology and personal circumstances. [3,4]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — What happens in the brain?
text: A helpful analogy: the brain is a network of cooperating systems, not a single on/off switch. That is why two substances, or two people using the same substance, may have different effects.

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Alcohol: immediate effects and longer-term risks
text: Alcohol contains ethanol, a psychoactive and toxic substance. It can interfere with neural communication and affect balance, memory, speech, judgment and reaction time. At high exposure, alcohol poisoning can impair breathing and consciousness. Its effects are not reliably judged by how confident or “normal” someone feels. [1,2]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Alcohol: immediate effects and longer-term risks
text: The WHO states that no pattern of alcohol consumption is completely risk-free. Risk varies with exposure and personal circumstances; many harms are concentrated in heavy episodic or sustained heavy drinking. [1]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Alcohol: immediate effects and longer-term risks
text: “I am not dependent, so alcohol cannot harm me.” Incorrect. Injuries, impaired judgment and some health risks can occur without dependence. [1]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — How different drugs act differently
text: The term “drugs” covers many different kinds of substances. Medicines can be useful when prescribed for an appropriate condition, but using another person’s medicine or combining substances can be dangerous. The categories below are broad and not a guide to consumption. [3-5]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — How different drugs act differently
text: Some effects interact. For example, alcohol used together with certain sedatives or opioids may increase the risk of dangerous breathing suppression. Someone should ask a qualified clinician or pharmacist about prescribed medicines rather than relying on social advice or a general learning page. [5]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Why age and life circumstances matter
text: Brain maturation continues through adolescence and into young adulthood. Alcohol exposure during this period may affect developing systems involved in decision-making, learning and memory. Earlier use and heavy patterns are associated with additional harms, but an individual outcome cannot be predicted from age alone. [2,6]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Why age and life circumstances matter
text: Risk also matters later in life. Medical conditions, medicines, work demands, pregnancy and other circumstances may change how a substance affects someone. In older adults, medication interactions and fall risk can be particularly relevant. A person’s vulnerability should not be judged solely by appearance. [1,5]

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Why age and life circumstances matter
text: Secondary school: A learner is told alcohol helps people become confident in public. A safe learning response is to explain that temporary feelings can coexist with impaired judgment.

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Why age and life circumstances matter
text: Musanze transport: A motorcyclist has been drinking and feels alert. The immediate safety lesson is not to drive or ride while impaired.

title: How Alcohol and Other Substances Affect the Brain and Body — Why age and life circumstances matter

Contact the relevant local emergency service or go to the nearest emergency department. Follow professional dispatcher instructions. Do not leave an unresponsive person alone while help is being arranged. [7]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Understanding risk without fear or stigma
text: A health risk is the possibility that an action or exposure may cause harm. The presence of risk does not mean harm is inevitable, and the absence of immediate symptoms does not prove a substance is safe. Alcohol and other psychoactive substances can affect thinking, reaction time, breathing, blood pressure, sleep and organ function. Some effects emerge quickly; other problems develop after repeated exposure or over years. [1-4]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Understanding risk without fear or stigma
text: Different substances have different mechanisms. Risk is affected by dose, potency, frequency, route of exposure, age, underlying health, prescribed medicines, substance combinations and the safety of the surrounding environment. Unknown or contaminated products add uncertainty. Avoid comparing risks using a single label such as “hard” or “soft” drug. [2,4]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Understanding risk without fear or stigma
text: Essential distinction: A person can experience poisoning, an injury or another serious event without having a substance use disorder. Conversely, someone with a substance use disorder may have harms that are not immediately visible.

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Immediate and cumulative harm
text: These columns describe timing, not severity. A short-term event can be fatal; long-term harms are not guaranteed. Both deserve attention. [1-4]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Alcohol: what may happen soon after drinking?
text: Alcohol contains ethanol, a toxic psychoactive substance. It can impair judgment, memory formation, reaction time, balance and coordination, even while a person feels confident. Some people become drowsy, impulsive, nauseated or confused. Greater exposure increases the likelihood of poisoning; severe poisoning may suppress breathing and consciousness. [1,3]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Alcohol: what may happen soon after drinking?
text: Alcohol can increase the likelihood of road crashes, falls, drowning and other accidents. It may contribute to unsafe decisions and interpersonal harm. Drinking in a situation involving driving, riding a motorcycle, operating machinery, supervising children or swimming introduces particular hazards. Risk exists before a person develops dependence. [1,3]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Alcohol: what may happen soon after drinking?
text: Combining alcohol with opioids or sedating medicines can intensify suppression of alertness and breathing. A clinician or pharmacist should advise on interactions with prescribed medicines. Never use someone else’s prescription or assume that mixing substances is safe. [3,6]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Alcohol: risks from repeated consumption
text: Over time, alcohol can damage the liver, contribute to hypertension and heart disease, affect the pancreas and digestive system, and increase the likelihood of alcohol use disorder. Alcohol has a causal link with several cancers, including cancers of the breast, liver, mouth/throat, oesophagus and bowel. Cancer risk may rise even with relatively low alcohol intake; drinking more generally produces greater risk. [1,5]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Alcohol: risks from repeated consumption
text: Alcohol may also worsen sleep and emotional difficulties. These connections are complex: anxiety or depression may contribute to substance use, and alcohol may worsen symptoms or interfere with care. Professional assessment should consider both. [1,3]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Drug-specific risks: understand the differences
text: The table is a simplified educational comparison, not a method to predict an individual outcome. Drug strength, contaminants, medical conditions, age and other exposures matter. Prescribed medicines have legitimate uses when taken as directed. [2,4,6,7]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Why young people require special care
text: Adolescence is a period of continuing brain and social development. Alcohol and other drug use during these years can impair judgment and safety, interfere with learning, and is associated with a greater risk of later substance-related problems. Frequent or heavy cannabis use in adolescence is associated with problems in memory, attention and functioning. Effects differ between individuals and do not justify labeling any student as “damaged.” [4,7]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Why young people require special care
text: Prevention should emphasize accurate information, supportive adults, school belonging, skill-building and confidential, age-appropriate help. Young people should never be required to reveal personal experiences to participate in educational activities.

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Additional situations that need care
text: Alcohol exposure during pregnancy can harm fetal development. People who are pregnant or planning pregnancy should seek professional advice about alcohol and other substances, including prescribed medicines, rather than changing treatment without guidance. [1,3]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Additional situations that need care
text: Certain health conditions, medications, changes in metabolism and fall risks can make exposure to alcohol or drugs especially hazardous. Medicine and substance interaction advice should be individualized by qualified healthcare professionals.

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Additional situations that need care
text: Someone may notice temporary relaxation, yet alcohol can disrupt sleep and make future stress or mood difficulties harder to manage. A short-term feeling of relief is not proof that a substance is treating the underlying problem. [1,3]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Additional situations that need care
text: Unregulated products may contain unexpected ingredients or strengths. Severe symptoms require urgent care; an online lesson cannot determine product contents or tell someone that an unknown substance is safe.

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Understanding use, harm, dependence and withdrawal
text: Use: consumption of a substance, which alone does not constitute a diagnosis. Harmful or risky patterns: exposure that causes or increases the chance of physical, psychological, social or safety problems. Substance use disorder: a clinically assessed pattern of problematic substance use and impaired functioning. Dependence and withdrawal: physiological and behavioral processes that may occur in some individuals and with some substances. These are related but not interchangeable terms. [2,8]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — Understanding use, harm, dependence and withdrawal
text: Withdrawal caution: A person who has developed physical dependence on alcohol or certain sedating medications may become seriously ill when stopping abruptly. Severe alcohol withdrawal can cause seizures or delirium. A qualified clinician should assess withdrawal risk; this chapter does not give a home detoxification plan. [8]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — When to seek urgent medical attention
text: Immediate danger: Seek emergency medical assistance for an unresponsive person, breathing that is unusually slow or irregular, seizures, severe confusion, collapse or other serious poisoning signs. Stay with the person when safe, follow emergency responder instructions, and do not wait for every symptom to appear. If available and an opioid overdose is suspected, responders may advise naloxone; medical help is still required. [6]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — When to seek urgent medical attention
text: Do not encourage vomiting, give coffee as a “cure,” or leave someone unconscious to sleep it off. If a person is unconscious but breathing, follow local emergency guidance for safe positioning and continued observation until help arrives. If they are not breathing normally, follow emergency dispatcher directions for resuscitation. [6]

title: Short-Term and Long-Term Health Risks of Alcohol and Drug Use — When to seek urgent medical attention
text: Someone concerned about alcohol or drug use can request a confidential health assessment before a crisis occurs. Encourage treatment without blame. People considering stopping alcohol after long periods of heavy use should discuss withdrawal risks with a clinician first. [8]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Start here: What will you learn?
text: A person may encounter alcohol or other substances through social life, prescribed treatment, curiosity, stress, or peer influence. These experiences should not be collapsed into one label. Understanding the terms helps us recognize health risks, communicate without stigma, and know when assessment is appropriate.

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Start here: What will you learn?
text: By the end of this topic, you can: distinguish key terms, recognize potential warning signs without diagnosing anyone, explain why tolerance and withdrawal do not automatically equal addiction, identify safe support options, and apply knowledge to fictional scenarios.

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Start here: What will you learn?
text: Core learning time: approximately 12–18 minutes, with optional activities. Learners can skip questions or go straight to help information. This time is an editorial estimate, not a measured result.

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — What does substance use mean?
text: Substance use means consuming alcohol or another substance. The term describes a behavior, not automatically a disorder. Substance use may carry health risks even if the person does not meet the criteria for addiction. For example, an individual may drink once and experience impaired judgment or an injury without having a substance use disorder. [1,2]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — What does substance use mean?
text: The context matters: a medication prescribed and used as directed is different from taking someone else's prescription for non-medical effects. A psychoactive substance can also be legal yet still pose important health risks. The educational goal is not to assign moral labels, but to understand possible effects and harm.

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — What does substance use mean?
text: "Misuse" is sometimes used for taking medicines differently from medical instructions or for use associated with harm. It can be unclear or stigmatizing when applied loosely to people. In reader-facing content, prefer specific descriptions, such as "taking someone else's prescription," "using more than prescribed," or "continued alcohol use despite harm." This improves clarity and avoids implying that every substance-use behavior is clinically identical. [2,3]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Risky and harmful substance use
text: Some patterns raise the likelihood of future harm: using a substance before driving, combining alcohol with sedating medicines, or repeated use in settings where judgment and safety are essential. Other patterns have already caused harm, such as repeated injuries, illness, or major disruption to school, work, or relationships. The seriousness of harm is not measured by whether someone appears dependent. [1,2]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Risky and harmful substance use
text: Example: A university student drinks heavily at a celebration and requires emergency assistance. The acute harm is important even if no dependence or ongoing disorder is identified. Another person may continue using a substance despite worsening health or family problems, which merits professional evaluation.

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Risky and harmful substance use
text: Risk does not equal diagnosis. A single incident can be dangerous; repeated problems can be a reason to seek care; neither should be used by a website to diagnose a person.

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — What are tolerance and physical dependence?
text: Tolerance describes a reduced effect from the same amount of a substance over time, or a need for more to obtain a similar effect. Tolerance can occur with some medicines even when taken appropriately and is not, by itself, proof of addiction. [3,4]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — What are tolerance and physical dependence?
text: Physical dependence describes physiological adaptation to repeated exposure. When a substance is suddenly stopped or reduced, withdrawal symptoms may occur. These can differ widely according to the substance, dose, duration, health conditions, and other medicines. Dependence can develop during appropriate medical treatment and must not automatically be equated with compulsive use. [3,4]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — What are tolerance and physical dependence?
text: Withdrawal is the set of physical or psychological symptoms that may occur following reduction or cessation of certain substances. Examples may include discomfort, sweating, sleep disturbance, or anxiety; some forms can be medically dangerous. Individuals should seek healthcare advice rather than abruptly changing prescribed medication or stopping heavy prolonged alcohol use without assessing withdrawal risks. [4,5]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — What does addiction mean?
text: In everyday language, addiction usually refers to a pattern in which a person continues using a substance despite harmful consequences, with difficulty controlling use. Clinicians more often use diagnostic terms such as substance use disorder or alcohol use disorder. Disorders vary in severity and should be assessed by a qualified health professional. [1,2]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — What does addiction mean?
text: Possible features considered during assessment include using more than planned, unsuccessful attempts to cut down, craving, continuing despite problems, neglect of important roles, hazardous use, and sometimes tolerance or withdrawal. No single sign proves a diagnosis. Symptoms, duration, context and impairment matter. [2]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — What does addiction mean?
text: The distinction is important for a person taking long-term prescribed medication: withdrawal symptoms after stopping do not necessarily mean they are addicted. Equally, an individual may show serious compulsive substance use without prominent physical withdrawal. [3]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Why problems can develop
text: Substance use disorders emerge from interacting biological, psychological, and social factors. Age of first exposure, individual vulnerabilities, stress, trauma, access to substances, peer norms, co-occurring mental health conditions, and the wider social environment may influence risk. These factors are not destiny, and none should be used to shame a young person or a family. [1,6]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Why problems can develop
text: Adolescence is a period of continuing brain and social development. Younger users should receive prevention-oriented, developmentally appropriate explanations and confidential, safeguarding-informed help when needed. The lesson must not invite children to share personal substance-use histories publicly or use a quiz as an informal screening process. [6]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Why problems can develop
text: Supportive relationships, safe school and community settings, credible information, coping skills, timely professional care, and prevention interventions based on evidence may lower risks. One-off warnings and fear-based campaigns alone should not be treated as sufficient prevention. [6]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Warning signs that merit attention
text: Potential warning signs include repeated difficulty cutting down, strong urges, missing important obligations, continuing use despite health or relationship problems, taking substances in unsafe circumstances, or increasing preoccupation with using them. Changes in sleep, mood or school performance may also be observed, but they have many possible explanations and must never be used alone to label a person. [2]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Warning signs that merit attention
text: A useful approach is to observe specific changes, invite an optional private conversation, listen without accusation, and encourage professional assessment when concerns persist. Protect children from punishment, humiliation, forced public disclosure, and avoidable stigma.

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Treatment and recovery: what help can look like
text: Substance use disorders are treatable health conditions. Care may include a structured assessment, brief intervention, counseling or other psychosocial treatment, medically supervised withdrawal when necessary, medicines for some disorders, management of co-occurring mental and physical health concerns, and continued community or family support. Treatment choice depends on the substance, clinical needs, available services, individual goals, and informed consent. [1,2]

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Treatment and recovery: what help can look like
text: Recovery is not identical for every person. Improvements in safety, health, family and work functioning, and sustained engagement with appropriate support may all matter. Recurrence of use can happen and should prompt reassessment of care rather than hopelessness or blame.

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Treatment and recovery: what help can look like
text: Rwanda's Health Sector Strategic Plan V (2024/25–2028/29) prioritizes improving access to quality healthcare and addressing important noncommunicable disease risk factors. This provides policy context, not proof that this educational module is approved or licensed by the Government of Rwanda. title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Safe and respectful family support
text: A family member may say: "I've noticed you missed several commitments and seem unwell. I care about you. Would talking to a health professional help?" This is generally more useful than accusations or threats. Offer practical support with appointments where wanted, protect privacy, and avoid forcing promises that are difficult to keep. If violence, acute intoxication, or serious medical symptoms are present, prioritize immediate safety.

title: Understanding Substance Use, Misuse, Dependence & Addiction — Safe and respectful family support
text: For minors, involve appropriately trained child-protection or healthcare personnel and follow applicable confidentiality and safeguarding rules. Do not suggest that a young person should solve a dangerous situation alone.
